(1842-1885)

PRESENTATION

by Fr. Ambrogio Eszer, O.P.,

General Relator

I.1. We were entrusted with the direction of the Cause of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore Orsi (1842-1885) on 1 June 2001. At that time, the Cause had at its disposal the depositions of 6 witnesses from an Ordinary Process, celebrated but not brought to completion, back in 1896, and a Diocesan Inquiry from the years 1995-2000, together with a large number of documents, partly archival, partly drawn from mass-media publications. From all these elements, the Postulator and external Collaborator, Rev. Sister Angela Florio, had prepared a good documentary base, with the sole defect of lacking a critical biography of the Servant of God, since until a few years ago such biographies were not given as much weight, especially in Causes begun under the previous legislation. Although this is not formally a historical Cause, we decided to present the Positio of the Cause to a Congress of Historical Consultors, for the following reasons: in the Ordinary Process only 6 witnesses were examined, whose depositions are fairly probative, since they had good knowledge of the Servant of God. Moreover, the Supplementary Diocesan Inquiry was celebrated more than 100 years after the death of the Servant of God; in it 26 witnesses testified, few of whom were "ex auditu a videntibus," and whose knowledge proved rather scarce. A possible Congress of Theological Consultors could plausibly reject the Positio, on account of the small number of eyewitnesses ("de visu"). In that case it would be necessary to resort to the Congress of Historical Consultors, celebrate a second Congress of Theological Consultors, and instead of two, three Congresses would have to be held. In truth, the Positio contains so much solid historical material that it is more than sufficient for a historical Cause. That said, it must be acknowledged that the depositions of the witnesses in the Ordinary Process are not lacking in appreciable evidentiary value. Taking into consideration the Index Table of Witnesses and of the Summarium concerning the 6 witnesses examined in that Process, it is shown that, of the 6 witnesses examined, those able to speak of the Servant of God's "Birth and family" numbered 1 (16.7%); of her "Secular life," 1 (16.7%); of her "Religious life," 5 (83.4%); of the "Heroicity of virtue," 6 (100.0%); of "(Heroic) Faith," 6 (100.0%); of "Hope," 6 (100.0%); of "Charity toward God," 6 (100.0%); of "Charity toward neighbor," 6 (100.0%); of "Prudence," 6 (100.0%); of "Justice," 6 (100.0%); of "Fortitude," 6 (100.0%); of "Temperance," 6 (100.0%); of "Poverty," 6 (100.0%); of "Chastity," 4 (66.7%); of "Obedience," 6 (100.0%); of "Humility," 6 (100.0%); of the "Supernatural gifts," 4 (66.7%); of "Illness, death and funeral," 6 (100.0%); of the "Reputation for holiness," 6 (100.0%); of "Graces and healings," 5 (83.4%). Of the 6 witnesses, 5.2 on average were able to testify virtually on all the questions, which corresponds to a percentage of 86.7%. The witnesses — namely 1 Bishop, 3 sisters of the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, and two secular priests of the Archdiocese of Palermo — appear to carry no small importance, especially considering the treatment that the Servant of God and her sisters suffered at the hands of certain secular priests in Florence. Nearly all the witnesses' depositions agree even in the various particulars concerning the heroicity of the virtues practiced by the Servant of God, leaving very little room for differences in the answers to the individual questions. By contrast, of the 26 witnesses in the Supplementary Diocesan Inquiry, which in reality is simply the continuation of the Ordinary Process, none was able to speak of the Servant of God's early years and family. Of her "Secular life" 4 witnesses spoke (15.4%); of her "Religious life," 4 (15.4%); of the "Heroicity of the virtues," 12 (46.2%); of "Faith," 2 (7.7%); of "Hope," 1 (3.9%); of "Charity toward God," 4 (15.4%); of "Charity toward neighbor," 10 (38.5%); of "Prudence," 1 (3.9%); of "Justice," 0 (0.0%); of "Fortitude," 3 (11.6%); of "Temperance," 2 (7.7%); of "Poverty," 3 (11.6%); of "Chastity," 0 (0.0%); of "Obedience," 2 (7.7%); of the "Supernatural gifts," 2 (7.7%); of "Illness, death and funeral," 1 (3.9%); of the "Reputation for holiness," 26 (100.00%); of "Graces and healings," 13 witnesses (50.0%). In conclusion, 4.9 witnesses on average were able to give an exhaustive deposition, that is, 18.9%. This result is naturally more than understandable, given that this latest Inquiry took place more than 100 years after the death of the Servant of God, and for the most part the witnesses were not directly informed by eyewitnesses. Nevertheless, it is of great interest to see which impressions survived despite this long lapse of time: the heroicity of the virtues of the Servant of God, at 46.2%; "Charity toward neighbor," 38.5%; "Humility," at 30.8%; the "Reputation for holiness," at 100.0%; and finally "Graces and healings," at 50.0% of the witnesses. This last figure would be quite surprising even in a process celebrated under entirely normal conditions. It confirms, besides the existence of a very strong reputation for holiness, the likewise very strong reputation for miracles, which in many cases proves rather weak.

I.2. Even though, because of the limited number of witnesses, their testimonies cannot carry the weight generally attributed to the usual, more extensive depositions, the validity of the contribution of the few witnesses examined there cannot be denied. The volume of the Summarium begins with the Interrogatoria Subpromotoris Fidei (A)1: these are the old Articuli, which have simply received a new name. The depositions of the witnesses examined in the two parts of the Process (B) are introduced by extensive headings and accompanied by very useful glosses2. The second part of the Summarium (No. II) begins with "Brief biographical notes on certain persons"3, which facilitate the study of the life of the Servant of God, in which they played a more or less important role but who are, otherwise, little-known figures. Among them is Emilia Laberiska, princess of Fitalia, also a friend of Blessed Mother Gattorno. Canon Luigi Ciaranfi, "persecutor" of the Servant of God, is presented rather briefly. Little information exists about his motives for acting against the Servant of God, although on the one hand he could have caused the near expulsion of the Servant of God from the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, while on the other hand he pursued conduct not infrequent in the 1800s. We have dealt, among other things, with the case of the Venerable Servant of God Maria Rosa Flesch, Foundress of the Franciscan Sisters of Waldbreitbach in the Rhineland, whose very existence, thanks to the precautions of a spiritual director, was concealed from the novices of the Congregation she herself founded. Such figures of tyrants toward meek religious women are found even today. Having gotten past this small prosopography4, we move on to examine section (A), that is, the "Personal documents of the Servant of God"5: the birth and confirmation certificates and the record of the recognition of the Servant of God's remains, a summary of her life, etc. Section (B), on the other hand, offers "Documents on the 'affair' of Florence"6, including an anonymous denunciatory letter, addressed to Blessed Rosa Gattorno and written in Tuscan dialect. The figure of Archbishop Eugenio Cecconi, whose predecessor, Gioacchino Limberti, had died on 27 October 1874, remains, at least in this part of the Positio, always in the shadows. Eugenio Cecconi (4 February 1834 - 15 June 1888) was a most learned man, a doctor in theology as well as in physics and mathematics, who was consecrated Bishop in Rome on 3 January 1875, having been appointed on 21 December 1874. As the historiographer of the First Vatican Council, throughout the whole controversy he does not appear to have moved from the Collegio Capranica in Rome, where he lived. We do not know whether there was an exsequatur from the Italian government7. In this way, the officials in Florence were in a position to act in the same way as Ciaranfi.

I.3. With section (C), a collection of letters of the Servant of God is brought to our attention, namely 78 of her letters known to the scholars who have examined them8, another authentic expression of the character of our Servant of God, especially of her humility. Section (D)9 contains the Votes of the Theological Censors, along with the Report of the Experts "in re historica." There is also a "List and presentation of archival and bibliographical sources" (A), as well as an "Evaluation of the sources for the purposes of the Process" (B). The latter in fact supports the Votum of the two Members of the Historical Commission, Cataldo Naro and Sister Roberta Frati. And we find "Documents on the reputation for holiness in life and in death of the Servant of God," which are divided into "Trial-related" and "Extra-trial"10. In these latter there are answered prayers and favors, various letters of remembrance, and also letters of the Servant of God and of Blessed Rosa Gattorno. The second-to-last section (F) contains some "Studies on the Servant of God"11. First we find a biography, written by Onorata Colli, friend of Blessed Rosa Gattorno, and dedicated to princess Emilia of Fitalia, whose generosity obviously had to be both honored and solicited at the same time. It is a simple work that makes no mention of the distressing events that befell Our Servant of God. The style follows a tendency toward apotheosis and, toward the end of the work, presumed healings are also mentioned. Another popular biography was composed by Roberta Cecilia Frati. This one too is edifying in tone, though it offers various pieces of information about the Servant of God's Florentine troubles. The Summarium is completed (G) by the Declaration of absence of (forbidden) cult.

II.1. In order to present to the scholars of the Cause a fuller picture of the person of the Servant of God and of the events surrounding her, the Petitioners thought of drafting an in-depth, that is, documented, biography, which was written by a historian of established repute, namely Count Ludovico Masetti Zannini. To tell the truth, the biography is based on extremely numerous documents, which from time to time are quoted in full. However, it is not a "documented" biography in the sense used by our Congregation, according to the commentary-document scheme. Even so, it must be noted that the Positio, even before the intervention of the distinguished scholar, already contained extensive documentary sections, so that the question inevitably arose: should all these documents be redistributed, dismantling the whole Positio drafted so far, creating new typographical errors, and so on? Fortunately, the solution found in our case has made the biography very agile, without diminishing its documentary value. Moreover, the Positio was compiled in a period when the biography was not yet considered as indispensable as it is today. It is preceded by a "Foreword" from the Postulation; by a "Preface," written by the Superior General of the Congregation of the Sisters, Daughters of St. Anne, Mother A. Maria Luisa Prandina; and by a "Presentation" by the late Fr. Master Dalmazio Mongillo, O.P. There follows a rich bibliography, divided into "Unpublished sources," "Published sources," and "Other publications and studies"12. In Chapter I, speaking of "The Family and the Setting"13, the distinguished author presents us with a detailed picture not only of the family of the Servant of God and her living conditions, but also of the economic and cultural situation of Albareto, her native village, which in the time of her childhood numbered no more than 926 souls. The people who lived there naturally had to remain very attached to an extremely traditional way of life, since for centuries the village belonged to the Diocese of Luni and Sarzana and later to that of Pontremoli. If nothing else, the author recalls, from different points of view, how the land of Albareto lacked development and any change except for a certain amount of emigration. The historiographer Don Tommaso Grilli says: "In general [the inhabitants] are frugal, industrious, not much given to amusements, but rather eager to acquire real property"14. In Chapter II, "A Still Living Tradition," the author moves from the general conditions to the individual ones of the Servant of God, whose virtues appear evident from her very childhood15. It happens that, after her entry into the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, and apart from condolences on the occasion of the death of a brother, Our Servant of God does not appear to have had further contact with her elderly mother and other family members, except with her sister, Sister Anna Fabiana, a member of the same Congregation. In Chapter III, on "The Call to 'A Greater Love'"16, the birth in the Servant of God of her religious vocation, that is, the call to convent life, is described. Chapter IV, "Prayer and Charity"17, tells of the Servant of God's spiritual journey toward the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, whose founding took place at Piacenza. Almost always newly founded institutes exercise a strong attraction on young Catholics, and this was also the case here. Chapters V-IX18 highlight the Servant of God's rise from novice to superior, from her activities at San Martinello (Perugia) to the founding of the house at Florence, the difficulties and progress, "renunciations and little flowers." Chapter X speaks of "The Harshest Trial"19, a subject continued in Chapters XI, "The Persecution Worsens," and XII, "Accusations and Defenses"20. As we have already noted, the case of the persecution of the Servant of God and her sisters by an ecclesiastical official, in the 1800s, is not unique of its kind. These events, like those surrounding the Venerable Servant of God Maria Rosa Flesch and the Servant of God Maria Francesca della Croce Streitel, demonstrate, among other things, that the persecution of the Church by the public authority does not always generate a strong, corporate resistance in charity among Catholics. This often happens because of continuous pressure and an overheated zeal that results from it, with the formation of groups that fight one another: that is, groups in power persecute others without power. In our specific case we are confronted with the strange spectacle of the Bishop of the Diocese remaining away from his own see for a long period, while his officials risk turning it upside down. Msgr. Eugenio Cecconi was a mild person, perhaps too mild, who helped, even materially, Blessed Maria Teresa Scrilli (1825-1889), but until 1878 he would not allow the reconstitution of the Carmelite Congregation founded by the Blessed. "A figure of great human and spiritual stature, Monsignor Eugenio Cecconi authored several extensive studies on the Council of Florence and its antecedents. Born in Florence in 1834, he was consecrated Bishop on 3 January 1875 and governed the Florentine Archdiocese until his death, which occurred on 15 June 1888, after a long and painful illness. Of a mild and charitable disposition, even to the point of sacrificing his own patrimony, he devoted great attention to the diocesan seminary and to the formation of candidates for the priesthood: his name is also linked to the completion of the façade of the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore, which had remained unfinished until then and which he inaugurated on 12 May 1887"21. With regard to the Sisters, Daughters of St. Anne, the Archbishop ordered the suppression of their house in Florence, then, following the intervention of certain influential persons, again allowed its existence. Blessed Rosa Gattorno "forgave" the Servant of God22, but one wonders: what was there to forgive? In the end it emerged that most of the slanders came from an unbalanced young woman, an aspirant sister at the Florence house, toward whom Blessed Rosa, from the very beginning, had felt "a strong repugnance"23. The only "fault" of the Servant of God was her failure to be wary of this young woman, "who had already done the same thing elsewhere, [while] the poor Superior Our Servant of God had to be admonished by the Archbishop." If, however, similar past conduct had been known to the archiepiscopal Curia, Canon Ciaranfi's behavior proves even more incomprehensible.

II.2. With Chapter XIII, "Return to Appignano"24, the "after Florence" period begins, reaching its unhappy climax with "The Gravest Humiliation," described in Chapter XIV25. The poisonous seed, sown by the Florentine official, produced among a group of superiors of the Congregation a strong movement in favor of removing the Servant of God from the Institute. Other superiors asked "mercy" for her, and in the end it was granted to her; yet here too the question arises: from what fault was she to be forgiven? That "mercy" proved partial, because the Servant of God was transferred to Ferrara, where she spent a period that was almost a punishment. It seems clear that the Foundress had chosen this compromise so as to prevent the sisters in Florence from speaking of a full rehabilitation, which would have further strengthened the animosity of Ciaranfi and his other friends. In short, it was a situation in which no one came off well, except the Servant of God, whose full rehabilitation at last — as superior of the "House of the Reformed Women" in Rome and then at Sermoneta, and as a nurse at Ovada — is described in Chapters XV and XVI26.

II.3. With the transfer to Palermo and her appointment as superior of the Congregation's new house in that city27, the last phase of our Servant of God's life begins. She arrived in the Sicilian capital on 4 May 1880. From May 1884 she was also provincial superior of Sicily, while keeping the post of superior of Palermo. Here, the distinguished biographer gives a detailed description of the conditions prevailing on the island, marked by the so-called "anticlerical" Piedmontism and by the reactions of those "liberated" from the Bourbon yoke. We have often wondered why Sicily was already so heavily neglected under the Bourbons, and we find no answer other than that, during the Napoleonic era, the royal family, living in Palermo, was protected by the English against the French, but also continually humiliated by the former. This must have created, in the dynasty, a strong aversion toward Sicily. Such considerations, however, have nothing to do with the story of the Servant of God, who found herself transferred to a difficult reality, marked by the sad poverty of the popular masses, which we had to study when dealing with the Causes of the Servants of God Francesco Paolo Gravina and Sister Vincenzina Cusmano. With his usual mastery, the distinguished biographer leads the reader into this world of horrors, also referring to more recent Italian literature, for example the works of Pelliciari. The distinguished author highlights the leading role of the Daughters of St. Anne in rebuilding charitable services in Sicily, after their total devastation at the hands of the Risorgimento. Difficulties in this process of integration could not be lacking in an environment that, because of Piedmontism, was hostile to foreign things. For this reason Chapter XVIII is devoted to "Integration into the Island"28. It must be said of the Servant of God and her sisters that they did not limit themselves to charitable work, but were always concerned with integrating that activity into a form of life, which is why Chapter XIX can speak of Sister Anna del Salvatore as a "Model of religious life"29. Chapter XX focuses on the difficult situation of the Servant of God and her sisters "Between the poor and benefactors"30. Chapter XXI reports on what might be called normality, that is, "Successes and obstacles"31. Among other things, we are informed that the Polish princess of Fitalia was not the only benefactress of high social rank, but that there was another, the princess of Belmonte, who together with Fr. Bova granted "a monthly allowance" for the community's support. As in Florence, so too in Palermo the Servant of God had to suffer because of certain shrewd letters from a sister of the Piacenza convent. Because of these letters, she temporarily lost the goodwill of the Archbishop of Palermo, Msgr. Celesia, and of his most authoritative collaborator, Canon Zuccaro. Fortunately this "misunderstanding" was soon overcome; nevertheless, it cannot be excluded that within the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne there lingered considerable misunderstandings among the sisters, probably because of the Institute's overly rapid expansion on the island. Chapter XXII in fact highlights "The Expansion on the Island"32, which made the appointment of the Servant of God as "Provincial Superior in Sicily" inevitable33. After that appointment, which took place in 1884, the Servant of God had to increase the number of her journeys and "undertake difficult travels with frequent discomforts." Her new dignity increased both her humility and her penances. To the hardships of travel were added epidemics, above all cholera. If the Servant of God and her sisters were not struck by the terrible disease, it is certainly because the sisters knew how to make the best use of personal hygiene. Even as provincial, the Servant of God had to suffer certain rumors, but unlike in the past, the sisters who spread such rumors had already left the Congregation. Chapter XXIV focuses on the "New Foundations"34. The Servant of God's appointment as provincial, even though it had not begun the movement of foundations, certainly reinforced it. The last three chapters, XXV-XXVII, inform us about "The Holy Death" of the Servant of God, which took place on 7 June 1885; "The Mourning and the Funeral Rites"35, where a spontaneous and strong reputation for holiness can be noted, and the subject "Defuncta adhuc loquitur" ("Though dead, she still speaks")36. Here, among other things, the history of the Cause is discussed, whose course was obviously conditioned by the Congregation's commitment to the beatification of the Foundress, Mother Rosa Gattorno, who had to overcome some very grave difficulties. The two World Wars, in any case, had no great influence on the progress of the Cause, because during the Great War no attack was launched against Sicily, and in the Second World War military actions were rather limited. However, beyond the Cause of the Foundress, the not entirely explicable delays in our own Cause are perhaps to be sought in the profound humility of the Servant of God, which constitutes the pivot of her life and of her virtues.

II.4. Turning our gaze for a moment to Part I of the Positio, that is, to the Informatio, we find, after the customary introduction, a "Biographical sketch of the Servant of God"37. Chapter I, instead, describes "The iter of the Cause"38. "The Proofs" are the focus of Chapter II39. As in the previous chapter, the Petitioners are careful here too to emphasize that the serious delay in the progress of the Cause involves no fault on the part of the Sisters, Daughters of St. Anne, which is in fact easy to understand given that the Acts of the first part of the Process, after exhausting searches, were found not in the archive of the Congregation but in that of the Archdiocese of Palermo. The documentary proofs are divided into sections of letters A-G, but those under letter E are in turn divided into two sections. It should be emphasized that, under letter D, we find not only the opinion of the two Theological Censors but also the report of the Members of the Historical Commission. Selections from the correspondence of the Servant of God are found under letter C. It must be acknowledged that this collection of letters, both of the Servant of God and of Blessed Rosa Gattorno and of other contemporaries of the former, is very thorough, covering the Servant of God's entire lifespan and, as we have already noted, already existing before the drafting of the Documented Biography.

II.5. The rest of the structure of the Informatio offers nothing further new. Chapter III addresses the "Heroicity of the virtues in general"40, Chapter IV speaks to us of the "Heroicity of the virtues in particular"41. The "Evangelical counsels and humility" occupy Chapter V, even though they too form part of the virtues42. The "Supernatural gifts" appear in Chapter VI43, the "Reputation for holiness and for signs" in Chapter VII44. As we have seen in the analysis of the Index Table of Witnesses and of the Summarium, the reputation for holiness and for miracles is extraordinarily strong. Chapter VIII introduces us to "The salient traits of the spirituality of Sister Anna del Salvatore"45 and is followed by Chapter IX on "The relevance of her Christian message"46. In our modest opinion, the greatness of the Servant of God is revealed above all in her humility, and this makes her a most timely figure, because in the modern world of fully emancipated man, humility has been not only forgotten but even disregarded, and the effects of such an orientation have unfortunately made their way even into sectors of the Church and of religious Orders and Congregations.

III. Therefore, having studied all the Acts of this Cause and all its historical sources, we are persuaded that no further research is necessary, holding that the material present in the Positio is more than sufficient for the Most Illustrious Historical Consultors and the Most Reverend Theological Consultors, afterward, to examine it for the purposes of their Votum on the validity of the historical research carried out by the Petitioners, as well as on the heroicity of virtue and the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore Orsi.

Rome, 25 March 2007.

Fr. Ambrogio Eszer, O. P.,

General Relator

ANNAE A SALVATORE

(in saec.: Mariae Annae Orsi)

Sororis professae Congregationis Sororum Filiarum a S. Anna

(1842-1885)

Super dubio

An constet de virtutibus theologalibus Fide, Spe, Caritate tum in Deum tum in proximum, necnon de cardinalibus Prudentia, Iustitia, Temperantia et Fortitudine, iisque adnexis in gradu heroico, atque de fama sanctitatis, in casu et ad effectum de quo agitur.

Your Eminences, Your Excellencies,

Reverend Consultors,

1. - We present today to your kind attention the humble, poor, and exemplarily holy figure of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore Orsi, a professed religious of the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, who in her life of barely 43 years (Albareto 1842 - Palermo 1885), 17 of which she lived as a religious, condensed a profound human and spiritual experience, confirming the reputation for holiness that had already surrounded her in life, and whose popular and spontaneous features, becoming ever more pressing, allowed for the opening in 1895 of the Ordinary Process, carried out in two distinct phases, though far apart in time (1896-1907; 1995-2000).

In now submitting, as is due, to the study of the Church this work on the life, virtues, and reputation for holiness of the Servant of God Sister A. del Salvatore, we consider it fitting to point out that it was reached thanks to the deepening and convergence of the essential sources of information: biographical (to which is now added a new, updated and documented biography by Prof. Masetti Zannini); documentary and procedural; and the support of other testimonies and sayings of the Servant of God, which were gathered and transcribed immediately, and then also over time, with meticulous and patient care, in order better to understand the meaning of her life experience as a model of holiness.

The exemplary nature of the episodes daily lived by the Servant of God throughout the whole course of her earthly life helps us to grasp well the peculiar traits of her service of charity and of governance, in which, fleeing from every appearance and seeking only the love of God and of neighbor, Sister A. del Salvatore knew how fully to give of herself, offering an authentic testimony of her humanity and conformity to Christ, as a most faithful servant obedient to the Church and to her Congregation.

In the encyclical Deus caritas est, Benedict XVI writes: "If I see with the eyes of Christ, I can give to others much more than their outward necessities; I can give them the look of love which they crave" (no. 18). Sister A. del Salvatore not only pursued love by her vocation, but made it truly her own spirit, so that it may well be said of her that she welcomed in humility the Lord's invitation to conform her heart and mind to his divine teaching.

A spirit of poverty, a fullness of humanity, a rejection of every form of abuse, falsehood, and compromise were joined in the Servant of God with love and the pursuit of true happiness: a great love for God and for others, carried out in the apostolic vocation complementary to the contemplative one, wherein, in total self-concealment and in an intense and profound bond of love, she immersed herself in God, remaining in ecstasy, in adoration, for hours and whole nights, thereby becoming all the more able to situate herself within the complex reality of her time, with the very heart of Christ and of the Church, and with the loving intensity and boldness proper to her foundress, Blessed Mother Anna Rosa Gattorno.

Wishing now to demonstrate that the Servant of God practiced in an exemplary and heroic manner all the Christian virtues and the duties inherent to her state of consecrated life, we shall follow her human and spiritual journey, structuring the present Informatio according to the following outline:

1. - Nine years after the death of Sister Anna del Salvatore, on 8 December 1894 a postulatory letter was addressed to the Cardinal Archbishop of Palermo, for the introduction of the Cause of the Servant of God, signed by numerous religious and civil personages (Proc., pp. 652-654; Summ., pp. 305-308).

The Ordinary Process, however, actually began on 2 September 1896 at the Curia of Palermo, and, some years later, on 5 January 1899, the Rogatory Process also began at the Curia of Pontremoli. But of this Rogatory Process it has not to this day been possible to find anything at all; as was also noted by the Report on the Ordinary Process attached to the 1995 request for the Nulla Osta (Proc., p. 72).

2. - The Ordinary Process at once suffered several interruptions.

a) After the second session, on 7 September 1896, the first interruption occurred, lasting until 1898. The Delegate Judge having died, the Postulator submitted, on 15 April 1898, a "Supplex libellus" (Proc., p. 111) and the "Notula testium" (p. 269). The Cardinal Archbishop then appointed the new Members, who, on the following 22 April, celebrated the third session.

b) Again interrupted after the VII session, the Postulator asked the S. Congregation of Rites for the faculty to set up a reduced Tribunal: a Delegate Judge, the Promoter Fiscal, and the Notary. The faculty was granted by Rescript of 6 June 1902 (Proc., p. 153).

The new "Supplex libellus" having been accepted, the Archbishop of Palermo, Card. Alessandro Lualdi, on 9 March 1905 appointed the Members of the Tribunal (Proc., p. 154).

c) At session XXIV, of 19 November 1907, the Process recorded yet another, far longer interruption, lasting until 1995 (1907-1995).

This interruption, since the Process had not been regularly closed, made it over time more difficult to locate the "Acts" of the sessions already held, which were found, after careful and persistent research, only in 1993.

3. - Despite the long period of time that elapsed — not through any negligence on the part of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, nor through fraud or deceit — the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore remained always alive not only among the Sisters of the Institute, but also in Palermo and in her native town (Albareto). So that the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne considered it fitting and necessary to resume and conclude the iter of the Cause, appointing a new Postulator (Proc., p. 4).

4. - On 8 March 1995, the Postulator of the Cause submitted a further "Supplex libellus" (Proc., p. 5) to the Archbishop of Palermo, Card. Salvatore Pappalardo, who, on 18 July 1995, requested — in conformity with the "Normae servandae" of 1983 — the Nulla Osta of the Holy See, obtained on 20 September of that same year, 1995 (Proc., p. 70).

5. - During the Ordinary Process, 24 sessions were held in all (Proc., pp. 84-269); and 6 eyewitnesses were examined, all of them qualified: a bishop, 2 diocesan priests, and 3 sisters of the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne (Proc., pp. 113-132; 155-269).

6. - The documentation of the Cause, which was not fully carried out at the time, supplemented by a series of documents gathered in that period by the Foundress herself, and later also by the Superiors General who succeeded her in governing the Institute, and by the various Postulators, was presented in the Supplementary Diocesan Inquiry, celebrated according to the "Normae servandae" of 1983.

7. - This Inquiry, likewise conducted at the Curia of Palermo, was organized into 37 sessions, from 26 July 1995 to 16 May 2000, with the examination of 26 witnesses, 2 of them ex officio, all de auditu a videntibus or de auditu ab auditu.

With the Process now concluded, the work was enriched by the addition of a suitable body of extra-trial documentation, now found in the archive of the General House, and considered useful for the sake of a fuller body of proof.

8. - The Decree for the resumption of the Cause — and for the conduct of the Diocesan Inquiry — as already stated, was granted on 18 July 1995. The Decree of Validity of the Process was issued on 2 May 2001.

For the verification of the Reputation for holiness of life, of the virtues, and of the miracles of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore, in Palermo, where She died in 1885, the Ordinary Process was celebrated in the years 1896-1907, and then, in the years 1995-2000, again at the ecclesiastical Curia of Palermo, a Supplementary Diocesan Inquiry on the continuation of the reputation for holiness.

Since the iter of the Cause of our Servant of God has been rather troubled, we consider it fitting to set forth a detailed supplementary account.

A. Testimonial Proofs

Ordinary Process

As we have said, and as can be seen from the dates given, the body of proof took a long time to assemble and was, as we wish to explain, rather laborious, with many interruptions due to reasons external to the Cause itself.

The reputation for holiness enjoyed by the Servant of God, both in life and in death, led the Foundress herself, Mother Anna Rosa Gattorno47, now Blessed, already in 1890, to take an interest in the Cause of beatification of her spiritual Daughter, appointing a Postulator in the person of Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro48, canon of the Cathedral of Palermo and secretary to the Archbishop.

Four years later, on 8 December 1894, nine years after the death of the Servant of God, a petition50 was addressed to the Archbishop of Palermo, Card. Pietro Michelangelo Celesia49, for the introduction of the Cause of the Servant of God. The petition was signed by 60 religious and civil personages, among whom were 3 Bishops, 33 Priests, the Prince and Princess of Fitalia51, and other noble personages. Among other things, this petition states:

"Merciful God, who had granted so many favors in life to His Servant, continues even after her death to glorify her, granting immense graces through the intercession of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi... the extraordinary graces continue to multiply, not only in the city of Palermo, but in very many regions of Italy and also of America."

On 1 March 1896, Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno appointed a new Postulator52, who, through his Vice-postulator, presented to the Cardinal Archbishop of Palermo the Supplex libellus for the introduction of the Cause. This request having been accepted, on 1 September 1896 the Cardinal Archbishop set up the Tribunal with the appointment of its various Members: Delegate Judge, Associate Judges, Subpromoter of the Faith, Notary, and Apparitor.

On 2 September 1896 the first Session was held, at which all the elected members took the prescribed oath. On 7 September, at the second Session, the Vice-postulator presented to the Tribunal the Articles and the List of witnesses. After this Session there was a first interruption; indeed, in fixing the date of the third Session it is stated: Sessio praedicta dilata fuit ex variis adiunctis usque ad diem 22 Aprilis 1898 ("The aforesaid session was postponed, for various reasons, until 22 April 1898")53.

On 15 April 1898, the Postulator submitted a new Supplex libellus with the List of witnesses54 for the resumption and continuation of the Process, and the Most Eminent Cardinal Archbishop appointed the new Members of the Tribunal, who took their oath at the third Session, on the following 22 April.

In Sessions IV-VII, from 25 to 29 April 1898, the first witness was examined, His Excellency Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, appointed Bishop of Caltanissetta.

After the seventh Session, the Process suffered a further interruption. The Postulator then asked the S. Congregation of Rites to set up a reduced Tribunal, namely: Delegate Judge, Promoter Fiscal, and Notary. The faculty requested was granted by Rescript of 6 June 190255.

The Postulator submitted a further Supplex libellus56 to the new Archbishop of Palermo, His Excellency Msgr. Alessandro Lualdi57, who on 9 March 190558 appointed the members of the reduced Tribunal, who took their oath at the eighth Session, of 17 April 1905.

The Process went forward as far as the XXIV Session, of 19 November 1907, when it was again interrupted, and for a very long period, that is, until 1995.

In the 16 Sessions held from 12 July 1906 to 19 November 1907, 5 witnesses were examined. We thus have, in this so troubled Ordinary Process, the examination of 6 witnesses in all, all of them eyewitnesses, who knew the Servant of God well throughout the whole period of her stay in Sicily. The second witness, Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, had already known the Servant of God at Piacenza.

On 5 January 1899 a Rogatory Process also began at the Curia of Pontremoli, but despite all the research carried out so far, it has not been possible to find anything regarding it.

It should be made clear at once that, in all the various interruptions of the Ordinary Process, up to its resumption, there never emerged any evidence of fraud, deceit, or negligence on the part of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

At first, the various interruptions were always due to the death of some Judge or Member of the Tribunal, not replaced in a timely manner. In addition, the considerable delay in resuming the Process after the last suspension was also due to the fact that the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, in 1927, had begun the Cause of beatification of the Foundress, Anna Rosa Gattorno. The search for the Acts of the Process, however, was never interrupted.

The Ordinary Process, because it was never regularly closed, made it very difficult over time to locate the Acts of the Sessions that had been held. The various relocations undergone by the archive of the Curia of Palermo further aggravated the situation; but careful, continuous, and persistent research led to the long-desired discovery only in 1993.

Diocesan Inquiry

Despite the time that had elapsed, the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore remained always alive among the Sisters, Daughters of St. Anne, in Sicily and in her native town of Albareto. Proof of this uninterrupted reputation for holiness is found, among other things, in the three exhumations of the body of the Servant of God, carried out over this long span of time for the sake of an ever better and more dignified resting place59. The Sisters, Daughters of St. Anne, therefore considered it fitting and necessary to resume the iter of the Cause.

On 5 March 1995, the Postulator submitted to the Archbishop of Palermo, Card. Salvatore Pappalardo60, the Supplex libellus for the resumption of the Process, through the celebration of a Diocesan Inquiry according to the new legislation of 1983.

Having obtained the Nulla Osta of the Holy See by the Rescript of 20 September 1995, the Cardinal Archbishop set up the Tribunal.

The Diocesan Inquiry was held in the years 1995-2000, in 31 Sessions altogether, chiefly concerning the continuation of the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God.

26 witnesses were heard, 2 of whom were summoned ex officio. They are all witnesses de auditu or de auditu a videntibus. The witnesses are: 3 priests, 11 Sisters, Daughters of St. Anne, 1 Sister of the Congregation of the "Missionary Sisters of the Good News," and 11 lay people.

Altogether, between the Ordinary Process and the Diocesan Inquiry, 32 witnesses were heard: 6 de visu, 18 de auditu, 8 de auditu a videntibus. Divided into categories, we have:

1 Bishop (I Ord. Proc.),

5 priests (III and IV Ord. Proc.; XVII, XX, XXV Dioc. Inq.),

14 Sisters, Daughters of St. Anne (II, IV, VI Ord. Proc.; I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, XIX, XXII, XXVI Dioc. Inq.),

1 Sister of another Congregation (XVI Dioc. Inq.),

11 lay people (IX, X, XI, XII, XIII, XIV, XV, XVII, XXI, XXIII, XXIV Dioc. Inq.).

As already stated, only the 6 witnesses of the Ordinary Process knew and dealt directly with the Servant of God. The witnesses of the Diocesan Inquiry testified concerning the reputation for holiness and its continuation to our own day, and concerning the fama signorum (reputation for signs).

B. Documentary Proofs

Every Christian is called to holiness. In the Apostolic Constitution Lumen Gentium, holiness is in fact seen as a norm flowing from the Christian vocation itself and as a legitimate requirement of it:

"All the faithful of Christ of whatever rank or status are called to the fullness of the Christian life and to the perfection of charity"62.

Throughout the whole course of her earthly existence, Sister Anna del Salvatore had no other aspiration than to become a saint, and she pursued this aim with all her strength. It is thus no surprise that all who knew her, directly or indirectly, agree in declaring that, throughout her whole life, the Servant of God scrupulously observed the commandments of God and of the Church, practicing every single Christian and religious virtue in a heroic manner.

For this life lived in an extraordinary and excellent manner, she is regarded as a model of an exemplary religious.

From the eyewitness testimonies of the Ordinary Process of Palermo, as well as from the documents on the continuation of the reputation for holiness, from the written testimonies, and from the many Reports, one can clearly grasp the heroic exercise of the virtues in general in a simple life wholly devoted to charity, such as was that of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, who had occasion to know her well, states as follows:

"... she was most observant, and in no ordinary way, of the Christian virtues"63.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, too, the second witness, declares:

"I can attest that I witnessed the exercise of many virtues of the Servant of God, which in my view have something of heroism about them. And by heroism I mean a virtue that is above the ordinary"64.

Likewise Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, attests:

"By heroic virtue I mean that which surpasses the ordinary, even that usually observed in pious persons. Now, as far as I could observe and sense, the virtues practiced by the Servant of God far surpassed the ordinary ones"65.

Sister M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, testifies:

"... the Servant of God was most perfect in every kind of virtue...

The virtues that the Servant of God practiced were of an extraordinary degree, above the ordinary run of good Christians and religious"66.

Fr. Giuseppe Palazzotto, the fifth witness, specifies and adds:

"By heroic virtue I mean that which surpasses the ordinary and the common. Now, that these virtues of hers were extraordinary can be seen from the way she practiced them. I can attest, for my part, that the Servant of God, in fulfilling her duties even while gravely ill, exerted herself in such a way that it was astonishing merely to watch her carry out certain most burdensome offices"67.

Sister Anna Serafina Gregory, the sixth witness, also an eyewitness, relates:

"By heroic virtue I mean a virtue that is above the common, the ordinary. Now, whenever I drew near the Servant of God, I saw how in her words and in her actions she truly blazed with love of God, like a Seraph. I saw in her a profound humility; she placed herself beneath everyone's feet. And this I saw and judged to be a true thing, never affected: sincere, as the Saints speak and act. This was the esteem that I and others had for the Servant of God"68.

The witnesses de auditu a videntibus heard in the diocesan inquiry likewise speak of the heroicity of the virtues of the Servant of God.

Sister Anna Margherita Tripi, the first witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, affirms:

"... I formed the conviction that the Servant of God was truly heroic in the exercise of the virtues and, in particular, in her submission to her Superiors, as well as in her great humility and in her generous dedication to the service of the poor."69

Sister Anna Teresina Lo Bue, too, the third witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, declares herself convinced:

"From what I heard said in the Community by the older Sisters, who spoke of the Servant of God as of a saint, I must hold that she practiced all the virtues to a heroic degree"70.

Likewise the Rev. Duilio Odoidio Schiavetta, the twentieth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, asserts:

"Ordinary life lived in a heroic manner, I believe, is the hallmark of Sr. Anna del Salvatore: her readiness toward her sisters and her total obedience toward her superiors even in conditions of precarious health. And, further, her spirit of sacrifice exercised in a heroic manner"71.

The Foundress, Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno, held the virtues of the Servant of God in such great esteem that in 1886, acting as spokesperson for the General Council, she asked the Archbishop of Palermo for the burial of the Servant of God in a holding place, basing the request on the heroic virtues practiced by Sister Anna del Salvatore within and outside the religious house, to which they bear witness.

"... The heroic virtues practiced by the Servant of God within and outside the religious house, accompanied by a humility at once simple and profound, with an impenetrable spirit of self-concealment..."72.

In the trial documents, too, the heroicity of the virtues of Sister Anna del Salvatore clearly emerges, virtues in which constant practice made the ordinary extraordinary.

In the letter sent to the Foundress on 7 July 1885, only a month after the death of the Servant of God, Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, writes:

"... Rev. Mother, I would not know how to describe in words the virtues which the late Superior possessed in a heroic degree; it was a hidden virtue, yet evident to all who came near her, even for the first time; in vain did she strive to conceal herself, to the point that, at certain moments and in certain cases, she tried to make herself appear ridiculous; this ingenious device was of no avail — she was the violet that spreads the fragrance of its scent while hidden beneath the leaves..."73.

Also in the circular letter sent to the whole Institute in January 1886, Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore, co-founder, and Mother Rosa Gattorno, foundress, attest:

"... She lived as a saint and died as a saint, a saint to such a degree as to give hope that one day God will glorify her with the honors of the altars.

In her all the virtues shone forth to a truly heroic degree..."74.

And in the report of Sister Anna Paolina Viani we further read:

"Her Faith, Hope, and Charity were very great; she also distinguished herself admirably in the practice of the other virtues, and in the spirit of mortification, penance, prayer, and union with God. She took great care, however, to hide from others' eyes her practice of all these virtues to so eminent a degree"75.

The entire existence of Sister Anna del Salvatore was thus characterized by a constant, extraordinary, and profound exercise of all the Christian virtues, which raised her simple and humble life to the dimensions of heroism.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church says of the theological virtues:

"The theological virtues are the foundation of Christian moral activity; they animate it and give it its special character. They inform and give life to all the moral virtues. They are infused by God into the souls of the faithful to make them capable of acting as his children and of meriting eternal life. They are the pledge of the presence and action of the Holy Spirit in the faculties of the human being"76.

Since these virtues animate and give moral activity its special character; since they inform and give life to the moral virtues; and since, finally, these virtues make us capable of acting as children of God and of meriting eternal life, being moreover "the pledge of the presence and action of the Holy Spirit" within our faculties, one understands the supreme importance they hold for our sanctification and the perfection of charity.

The Church, therefore, in these specific Causes, wants the candidates for the honors of the altars to be carefully examined as to whether they were truly heroic in the exercise of these virtues, so that they may be proposed as models to the whole people of God.

a) Heroic Faith

Faith was the essence of the spiritual life of Sister Anna del Salvatore. Attracted and won over by Christ, the Servant of God opened herself unconditionally to His love, and, letting herself be shaped by the Spirit, made her life a continual sacrifice of praise to the Lord, in whose presence she lived continually, though she sought, through various devices, to conceal this. All her conduct was the reflection of her constant interior recollection and her intimate union with God, especially in the most difficult and painful moments that crossed her life. The Servant of God, in all her actions, manifested a great and heroic faith, such as to leave a mark on people's hearts.

In her conversations, too, as in her correspondence, the Servant of God revealed her adherence to Christ and unfailingly called to mind sentiments and thoughts of faith. It could be seen and understood that her whole life was a constant and unceasing pulse of the most ardent, most deeply rooted, and most heartfelt faith, which guided and animated her in thinking, in acting, in working.

The first Theological Censor of the writings of the Servant of God writes:

"From reading the letters in chronological, progressive order, three stages can be discerned in the growth of this virtue, corresponding to the various moments of the Servant of God's Christian and apostolic growth. The first stage concerns the expression of faith as abandonment to providence. This matures in a second moment, defined by recourse to unceasing prayer. The letters of the last period of her earthly existence show a unitive stage of the Servant of God with God and the Church"77.

The second Censor notes:

"From her youth she knows the taste for prayer, which becomes the inexhaustible source of her life, to the point that she cannot resist the Lord and finds no further consolation in this world. Prayer grows with her and takes on the coloring of the various needs and seasons of the Servant of God's life, but it is always an expression of total availability and full trust in God's provident intervention in her own life, in that of the Institute, of those she assists, and of those who turn to her for every need. The numerous difficulties and trials she encountered are all borne and resolved in long hours of adoration before the Sacrament, which instill in her courage and optimism; these sentiments she passes on to her correspondents, managing to put to death within herself every negative feeling, or even a simple discouragement"78.

The Historical Experts, in their report, specify concerning the faith of the Servant of God:

"The spirit of prayer is the most genuine expression of faith. Faith led the Servant of God to cleave to her Lord and to seek an ever fuller communion with him. From the documents and testimonies it emerges that her whole life was a continuous dialogue with the divine Persons of the Holy Trinity. And it was this prayer that made her ready to do God's will in the various circumstances of her existence... The relationship with God learned within her natural family and her parish family, in which she felt herself an active member, became ever more personal and intimate"79.

All this is confirmed for us when we listen to what is said in this regard by those who knew her or dealt with her in the various phases of her human journey.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, declares:

"... as to her faith, I believe that she practiced it continually in the presence of God, the night not excluded; although, through various devices, she sought to conceal this"80.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, asserts:

"I can attest, both from having heard it said and from my own experience, that the Servant of God was most observant not only of what concerns the law of God and the Precepts of the Church, but also of the duties and rules of the holy Institute"81.

And she adds:

"I can attest that the faith of the Servant of God was truly admirable.

As to the Servant of God's dispositions regarding her wish that faith in God be spread everywhere, I can attest to this for the time during which I knew her.

As to devotion to the Blessed Sacrament, I attest that the Servant of God was a true adorer, and likewise toward the Blessed Virgin, toward St. Anne, and toward the Saints of God in general.

I know for certain that the Servant of God respected the Ministers of the Lord and was most devoted to the Pope, to whose wishes she said she was ready to obey.

... the Servant of God was most devoted to the Souls in Purgatory.

... the Servant of God had great zeal in instructing in matters of faith the young people entrusted to her"82.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, reports:

"Her most lively faith was revealed in every action and word of hers... I was told by the Sisters that she would spend whole nights behind the altar of the Blessed Sacrament, in adoration, in their own private Chapel. She always aspired to the eternal possession of her beloved God, which was the sole goal of every one of her actions"83.

The Servant of God was a profoundly meditative soul (and this is another aspect that makes her heroic exercise of faith all the more evident); at any moment of the day, she was always present to meditation on the mysteries of our faith.

Mrs. Maria Tomaselli, the thirteenth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, declares:

"It was said in the village that, from girlhood, the Servant of God was very good, prayed continually, and went to pray even at the cemetery at night"84.

From a very young age, she was most punctual in attending Holy Mass every day and, as far as she could, always took part in sermons, religious services, and novenas. She was eager and solicitous in accompanying the Viaticum to the sick. Significant in this regard are the testimonies drawn from the written reports. As early as 1890, the Parish Priest of Albareto (the birthplace of Sister Anna del Salvatore) wrote:

"With devotion she frequented the holy Sacraments and with devotion said her daily prayers. At novenas and feasts of devotion she never failed to come to Church, and she took part in accompanying the Viaticum to the sick and in funeral processions for the dead"85.

As mentioned above, the Blessed Eucharist was her principal devotion, and all her other devotions were subordinated to it. Every moment left free from her occupations, Sister Anna del Salvatore in fact spent at the foot of the altar, before the Blessed Sacrament.

"She would spend every free moment of the day before the Blessed Sacrament, and often whole nights or a great part of them; in prayer, frequently, especially after receiving Holy Communion, she would remain absorbed, to the point of not noticing what was happening around her"86.

Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, testifies:

"Concerning devotion to the Blessed Sacrament, I heard the Sisters say a great many things: they also said that she would spend whole nights in the Chapel before Jesus in the Sacrament. Toward the Blessed Virgin, too, she nourished a filial devotion."87

Likewise, Fr. Giuseppe Palazzotto, the fifth witness, maintains:

"... in her shone a great faith in God, and I was told by the Sisters that the Servant of God would spend whole nights before the Blessed Sacrament, seated on the step of the Altar"88.

Fr. Gaetano Gabriele, in the funeral oration at the obsequies of the Servant of God, says:

"A lover of the worship of the Lord, she desired and obtained that the Blessed Sacrament be exposed frequently, regarding the day of exposition as a day of paradise; for then she could better linger in sweet converse with the blessed Jesus"89.

In the Supplementary Diocesan Process of Palermo, too, there are some testimonies that show the great spirit of faith of Sister Anna del Salvatore and her intense and most particular devotion to the Eucharist.

Sister Anna Vincenza Lo Bue, the fourth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, attests:

"Among the most significant facts of her life and among her virtues, I especially admired her spirit of prayer and penance. Indeed, I learned that during the day she carried out her duties, while she spent the night hours before the Blessed Sacrament and, when overcome by sleep, rested by stretching out on the very step of the altar."90

Mrs. Bice Borella, the fifteenth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, reveals:

"I learned from my parents that Sister Anna del Salvatore, even in winter, would kneel and, braving the cold, would pray for a long time on the bare floor"91.

Sister Anna Nazaria Provera confirms:

"Such was the faith of the Servant of God that she would pray at length before the Blessed Sacrament, spending whole nights there, in any season of the year. She exhorted us, her subordinates, to seek in God our only comfort. She heard Holy Mass with profound recollection, as well as the community prayers, meditation, the Sacraments, etc..."92.

Following the example of the Apostle Paul, who wished to know and love nothing but Jesus, and him crucified (cf. 1 Cor 2:2), the Servant of God was set aflame with love whenever she spoke of the sufferings of Jesus Christ, and with inspired words she sought to instill in the souls of her listeners devotion to the mysteries of the Cross.

Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte confirms this for us:

"So great was the love the Servant of God bore her Jesus that it is hard to say whether every minute of the day she gave him thanks for having had her born within the bosom of the Church and of Catholic parents. With fearless candor she always showed everyone that she firmly believed every article of the Faith and the most sublime Mysteries... She prepared to celebrate the feasts with works of piety, then with fasts and penances. One cannot describe the devotion and recollection with which she remained before Jesus in the Sacrament. Her heart seemed as though it would melt, so tender and fervent — indeed fiery — were the acts of love, sorrow, and humility she offered him. Her fervor was immense when she heard Holy Mass and frequented the Sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist. She was most devoted to the Passion of Jesus and spoke of it with such expressiveness that she kindled the fervor of all who heard her. She instilled this devotion in everyone, especially the sick, whom she led to regard their sickbed as the Cross of Jesus and to offer him their painful infirmities"93.

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari emphasizes:

"... Perhaps no one more than she blessed having been born within the bosom of the Church and of Catholic parents; simple in each of her beliefs, yet so firm that never did a shadow of doubt seem to cloud the articles of the Faith and the most sublime mysteries. She had a wholly particular devotion for the Blessed Sacrament: the altar was the refuge of her tribulations, her rest in life's long struggles, her haven of peace and her nighttime repose. And there, beside it, with what liveliness of faith she implored from God help in her needs, and in those concerning the whole Community.

To Jesus in the Sacrament she poured out her anguish, her many sorrows; she asked with confidence to obtain, and with the trust that love alone can give, infinite graces and favors for all who were in need of them. And how many graces her saintly Faith did not obtain! Her bed was the steps of the altar, for her night was made for nothing but prayer, whether before the Tabernacle or at the bedside of the sick, where she often went to keep vigil.

... The Mass, that sublime Sacrifice, was felt by her Soul, which was lifted up in It, made one with the great Act which she deeply grasped, communing with the Love she pressed to her breast, burning with fervor, through the Holy Eucharist, on which she fed daily with rapture and humble devotion. Often, and with compunction, she also approached the Sacrament of Penance, filled with sorrow for her faults..."94.

Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi reports:

"... If she had a little time, she spent it before the Blessed Sacrament, for she was found again and again, both day and night, with her face to the ground on the step or behind the altar, praying, and she seemed like a seraph; she prayed as long as she could, heard Mass with such devotion... she went to confession every eight days and, whenever she needed advice about something, went more often; she said that Jesus had to enlighten her so that she might do her duty well — such was her faith in confession.

When she approached Holy Communion, which was daily, she remained as if in ecstasy, her face all joyful, and one could see she was speaking with the Lord... she respected the church, and when she was in the Chapel she would not allow anyone to speak of anything at all; she would say, if you need something, call me outside, but not in the Chapel, because it is a lack of respect toward Jesus"95.

Wholly given over to her Spouse, sustained by faith, comforted by prayer, open to the provident intervention of the Father, docile to counsel and spiritual help, Sister Anna del Salvatore advanced step by step along the path of perfect abandonment to the heart of God, letting the Spirit's action form within her the very features of the Only-begotten Son, in whom the Father has placed all his good pleasure.

She had, moreover, a special devotion, which she sought to spread by every means, to the Most Holy Virgin, to St. Anne, and to all the Saints of Paradise, to whom she commended herself in her anguish.

"As to the Servant of God's devotion to Our Lady, I know this for certain and attest to it. She had a small image of Our Lady, toward which she had a particular devotion"96.

Sister Anna Del Consiglio Chiaramonte, in her Report, further writes:

"She showed a most tender affection for the Blessed Virgin, calling upon her often during the day by the sweetest and most tender names and titles... Very great was the love she bore toward St. Anne, our glorious Mother, and with what devotion and with what pious exercises she prepared every year to celebrate her feast!... She likewise professed great devotion to St. Joseph, to St. Michael, and to the Guardian Angel, and when she instructed children or the unlettered, she urged upon them devotion to these beloved Saints, especially to the Most Blessed Virgin"97.

"She loved the holy Virgin with the tenderest love," notes Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari, "oh, how much fervor her bearing inspired when she prayed before the beautiful image of Our Lady, still kept in the Provincial House of Palermo! How many times, in difficult moments, was she seen prostrate before Her, with the force of an invocation that insistently seeks help, light, or courage!"98.

The Servant of God had great respect and veneration for the Pope, for the Church, and for the whole ecclesiastical Hierarchy. She obeyed scrupulously the laws of the Church; she respected the Priests and all Superiors, always showing herself respectful and obedient toward them; she was most zealous for worship and for the decorum of sacred things.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, declares:

"I know for certain that the Servant of God respected the Ministers of the Lord and was most devoted to the Pope, to whose wishes she said she was ready to obey"99.

Sister Anna Nazaria Provera further reports:

"She held in great veneration the Supreme Pontiff, the Prelates, and the other Priests.

I sometimes saw her pay homage to His Eminence Cardinal Celesia with such a sense of faith that she prostrated herself to the ground, kissing his sacred ring, with the greatest veneration. She was most zealous for the decorum of the church, striving to adorn it with great care, as a sign of love for the house of the Lord"100.

Likewise Sister Anna Del Consiglio Chiaramonte continues, in her report:

"She was very attached to the laws and prescriptions of the holy Church, and thus bore toward it a holy veneration; most respectful toward the head of the Church, that is, toward the Supreme Pontiff, toward the Bishops, and toward all Priests, whom she regarded as the very person of Jesus Christ... She was also most zealous for the decorum of the house of God, caring above all for silence, composure, and recollection, and then for the jealous care of the Sacred Vessels and other furnishings"101.

And Sister Anna Crocifissa Fiocchi confirms:

"She was most zealous for the worship of God; with such care she kept everything belonging to the chapel. She always showed such reverence and obedience to her Superiors; she esteemed everyone more than herself: she was never heard to utter an offensive word against anyone, and always held herself to be the last of all"102.

Persevering to the end in the practice of the faith, Sister Anna del Salvatore, by her very life, spoke to everyone of the universal goodness of God and of his boundless readiness to forgive, and, like a pinch of leaven in the dough of the world, she influenced others without many words.

It is, indeed, the unanimous voice of all who knew the Servant of God, directly or indirectly, that she showed the ardor and firmness of her faith in the constant effort and the most zealous care she devoted to ensuring that her Sisters, the residents, the young women, and the children in the houses over which she presided, were thoroughly instructed in Christian duties and in everything the faith teaches and the Church proposes for belief. This care and zeal bore most abundant spiritual fruit103.

b) Heroic Hope

"Hope is the theological virtue by which we desire and await from God eternal life as our happiness, placing our trust in Christ's promises and relying on the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit in order to merit it and to persevere to the end of our earthly life"104.

On the one hand, therefore, hope prolongs the act of faith's adherence in the desire for future goods; on the other, it is the virtue of man on his way toward eternal life who, during this journey, experiences the difficulties of life and the risk of not reaching the desired goal. Hence trust in the grace of God, which will make it possible to overcome every difficulty.

Of our Servant of God Anna del Salvatore it can rightly be said that she lived this dynamic of Christian hope in a distinctive way, and lived it heroically throughout her life up to the moment of her death, as we can gather from the testimonies and above all from the documents.

Animated by supernatural hope, in every circumstance Sister Anna del Salvatore placed great trust in the grace of God and in the intervention of divine Providence, and, certain that the Lord would never abandon her, in need, in sorrow, in tribulations, in the most difficult cases, in every event she showed that she rested tranquilly in the bosom of Him from whom she received and hoped for everything, and, sustained by this hope, she did and endured all things.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, testifies:

"... I can affirm her immense trust in divine Providence: so much so that she was never distressed by the urgent needs of life, giving no importance at all to the money she received"105.

"I confirm the state of calm that the Servant of God preserved at the extremity of her life"106.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, too, the second witness, observes:

"... it is true that she was animated by this virtue of hope.

I know personally of the great trust the Servant of God had in everything.

... that she did not lose heart or grow discouraged at the obstacles that stood in the way of her works of zeal, I can attest to this.

As to her trust in God at the point of death, or her tranquility, I attest to this with certainty"107.

Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, declares:

"From her actions one could see that she acted with a view to attaining eternal life"108.

"... The dispositions of the Servant of God in her final illness made death something to be desired, such were the ardent longings of her heart and the confidence she had of flying to the bosom of the Lord"109.

Fr. Giuseppe Palazzotto, the fifth witness, confirms:

"... I heard from her own lips with what ardent longing she yearned for Heaven, and how, in every circumstance, she placed all her trust in God alone"110.

Sister Anna Serafina Gregory, the sixth witness, maintains:

"I heard it told how the Servant of God, amid the difficulties that confronted her, had immense trust in the Lord"111.

Of how great her hope was, the Servant of God herself always gave clear proof, especially amid anguish and suffering. In the difficult offices entrusted to her, she often had to face obstacles that seemed insurmountable: at times she saw the Community lacking necessary things, the grave responsibilities entrusted to her frightened her, but, by resorting to prayer and trusting in God, she always experienced his fatherly and provident help, and in him she always overcame everything.

Writing to the Foundress Mother on 16 March 1877 from Florence, she reveals the following to her:

"Dear Mother, as to those 80 francs, I beg you not to trouble yourself about it... I beg you to stay calm, for Jesus will provide for the Sisters' departure, because he is my treasurer, so I think of nothing, because Jesus sees that I am an untamable little donkey, and so he thinks of everything. Yesterday the bread bill came to me and I began to laugh, because I had only 30 francs and the bill was nearly 90 francs, but the Lord, so good, provided me with that and even more... So I am happy, because I think of nothing"112.

In the trial documents, too, this firm hope in the Servant of God is clearly shown.

Sister Anna Nazaria Provera — who lived with the Servant of God in Palermo in 1884 — reports:

"Being at the head of a numerous community, in the city of Palermo where the Sisters had to live on alms, she did not worry about temporal things, she hoped solely in God, exhorting us Sisters not to worry, even in difficult cases, confident that the Lord will never fail those who trust in him. She was of frail health, yet in spite of this she undertook any labor, trusting that the Lord would grant her the strength needed to bear the burdens of the office of Mother Provincial over all of Sicily"113.

Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte attests:

"The Servant of God always showed that she held the lowest opinion of herself, to the point of believing herself a great sinner, yet she firmly hoped to obtain eternal salvation through the infinite merits of our Lord Jesus Christ.

She never worried about nor showed excessive concern for temporal things; she hoped always in God, even in the most difficult and unforeseen circumstances, redoubling her prayer and her fervor and, serene and calm, awaited the happy outcome. She suffered always, and at all times, slanders and persecutions such as would weaken and terrify souls endowed with solid and robust virtue. But the Servant of God never lost her peace of mind, nor the peace of her conscience; she always showed herself calm and serene both in favorable and in adverse circumstances, and always prayed for her most relentless persecutors.

She was often visited by her dear and loving Jesus with quite painful illnesses, but she always bore them with unfailing patience; indeed she seemed to rejoice in them, for her face appeared more cheerful than usual. All her desires, every breath of her heart, were turned toward heaven; hence in her conversations there was talk of nothing but God and heaven, kindling even the hardest hearts and moving them to such wholesome desires. With such and so great a tenor of perfection in her life, it can well be understood, and it is no wonder, that the Servant of God obtained from her beloved spouse Jesus graces and favors, and even the gift of miracles, as a reward for her heroic hope"114.

Sister Anna Maristella Calderone asserts:

"... she trusted fully in her God, whose mercy and help she invoked both for the needs of her own soul and for the growth of the Institute, which she loved tenderly. And from this full trust in God there was born in her that admirable peace of heart and that readiness to conform to the divine will"115.

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari, too, emphasizes:

"The Hope of Sister Anna del Salvatore often shone forth, with the impulses of her heart fixed on the Eternal Good, in every small trial that the Lord was pleased to send her: not that she firmly hoped for eternal salvation through Our Lord's merits — that goes without saying — but in temporal matters, in the most difficult or unforeseen cases, she committed everything to the foot of the Sacrament, and then her living Faith sweetly answered with the Hope of a swift relief..."116.

Her heroic hope shone forth clearly in the painful episode of Florence, where the Servant of God had been unjustly accused and slandered. Yet always she showed herself calm and trusting in the Lord's help.

Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi confirms:

"She had immense adversities, even from her own superiors, especially from a certain Fr. Andreotti of Florence, who went so far as to slander her by saying she was opposing the Foundress Mother, whereas I can say in good conscience that she held her in the veneration she deserved; the poor woman bore all these terrible adversities, even to the point of being stripped [of the habit], but she, with the utmost resignation, always trusting in God, [was certain] that the habit would never leave her..."117.

During the spiritual exercises of the Superiors of the Institute, in the course of which decisions had to be made concerning her, the Servant of God confided to Sister Anna Elisabetta Veronesi:

"'This morning I went to confession, I made Holy Communion in the Holy House; let happen what will, I am at peace and wholly given over to my Lord'... not a word of excuse or defense left her lips; rather she said to me, 'Ah! if the Lord did not keep his most holy Hands upon my head, I could do this and worse'; and, giving herself wholly into the hands of the Lord, she entrusted her defense to him"118.

Sister Anna Raffaela Ceruti emphasizes in her report:

"Her hope was in God alone; in the most difficult cases, she was always cheerful and content with what God disposed for her; in the face of slander she kept silence, and in prayer, always the same; threatened with punishment, she did not change her manner; indeed, in those difficult moments, she seemed to unite herself more closely to God, so much so that it seemed not to be she who suffered such anguish; and this persuades me of her innocence, that she suffered everything out of love for God and for justice"119.

This heroic virtue appeared evident in the last moments of her life. With serene tranquility and a smile on her lips, she went to meet death, for she firmly hoped to attain eternal beatitude through divine goodness and mercy and through the infinite merits of Jesus Christ.

In this regard, Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, who attended the Servant of God in death, says:

"She always aspired to the eternal possession of her beloved God, which was the sole goal of every one of her actions"120.

Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, affirms:

"I went to visit her every day, and I was able to observe her tranquility and resignation; indeed, she showed herself content to die..."121.

To so many testimonies there echoes still Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari, who, in the Report already cited, convinced of the Servant of God's heroic hope and of her sanctity, already invokes the intercession of Sister Anna del Salvatore for herself and for all the Sisters:

"O holy Soul, give us a spark of Your hope that may shine in our hearts as when You spoke of Your longings for Heaven; give us the smile that, in every event, may make us rest tranquilly in the bosom of Him from whom You yourself hoped for everything!"122.

c) Heroic Charity

St. Thomas, speaking of the theological virtues and their relevance for the sanctification of the Christian, observes:

"Faith points out the end, hope makes us desire it, charity attains it" (St. Thomas, in Tim. 1,2).

By its nature, then, charity holds primacy over all the operative capacities of our spiritual being. This claim is confirmed by the common doctrine of the Church, grounded in Pauline teaching and thus summarized in the Catechism of the Catholic Church (no. 1827):

"Charity is the theological virtue by which we love God above all things and our neighbor as ourselves for the love of God. Jesus makes it the new commandment, the fullness of the Law. It is the 'bond of perfection' (Col 3:14) and the foundation of the other virtues, which it animates, inspires, and orders: without it 'I am nothing' and 'I gain nothing'" (1 Cor 13:1-3).

Fully convinced of this, the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore, just as she firmly believed and hoped, so too loved God with her whole heart, with all her strength, with her whole soul, and consequently loved her neighbor as herself.

Love of God

From infancy, the Servant of God showed a strong attraction toward God, and expressed it in a particular way on the day of her first communion. Her great love for him was revealed in the scrupulous observance of the Commandments, the evangelical Precepts, and the Rules of the Institute. Another intense expression of her love for God was prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. Moreover, Sister Anna del Salvatore always took the utmost care to keep herself far from anything that might in even the slightest way offend the Lord, while always ready, on the other hand, to make reparation through her penances for the offenses committed against God.
