From the eyewitness testimonies it appears very clearly how the virtue of charity toward God is, in Sister Anna del Salvatore, the most luminous and significant.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, testifies:

"As to her charity toward God, it seemed to me that she was truly imbued with it, which I gathered from what I have already said... indeed, I consider that it was no ordinary charity, because she let nothing of her interior show through, but I could grasp it from certain of her expressions. For, with priests, out of a spirit of humility and deep respect she did not reveal herself, expecting instead from them some word of the spirit"123.

And Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, confirms:

"As to the love the Servant of God bore for God, I can attest to it: she was always aflame with this divine love.

As to the observance of the Divine Precepts and of all her other obligations, I can attest to it.

... I know for certain with what ardor she received Holy Communion every day while she was in religious life.

... it is true what is said of her devotion toward the Blessed Sacrament: she spent whole nights before the Tabernacle, in a true spirit of most loving ecstasy.

As to her generosity in suffering for God, I attest to it from my own experience"124.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, adds:

"Of her ardent love for God everyone spoke, and I myself perceived it frequently. The Sisters told me that she would spend whole nights behind the altar of the Blessed Sacrament, in adoration, in their own private Chapel. She always aspired to the eternal possession of her beloved God, which was the sole goal of every one of her actions"125.

"I confirm the ardent desire of the Servant of God to suffer for Jesus Christ"126.

Fr. Giuseppe Palazzotto, the fifth witness, points out:

"Charity in her was ardent, being always aflame with the Divine Love: she always spoke like a Seraph"127.

Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, declares:

"... in general one could see how she conformed herself to the divine designs.

From the course of her actions one could see how, and how much, the Servant of God loved the Lord..."128.

Sister Anna Serafina Gregory, the sixth witness, attests:

"Now, I, whenever I drew near the Servant of God, saw how, in her expressions and in her acts, she truly blazed with the love of God, like a Seraph"129.

Aware that the love of God is the one true treasure, Sister Anna del Salvatore let herself be worked upon by the Lord, and, in humble and attentive fidelity, docile in listening to his voice, was always ready to do his will.

In the reports written by her spiritual daughters one finds an admirable, unanimous, and firmly convinced testimony concerning the love the Servant of God bore toward the Lord.

Sister Anna Crocifissa Fiocchi notes:

"When she saw God offended, she would exclaim: either Paradise or the desert. So ablaze was she with the desire to be united with God. In attending Holy Mass and in receiving Jesus in the Sacrament into her heart, she remained so deeply recollected"130.

In Sister Anna Nazaria Provera we read:

"She observed the laws of the church with exactness, to the point of scrupulousness. She avoided every, even the smallest, offense against God. In her bearing one could perceive a heart inflamed with the love of God. When questioned, she answered in few words, so as not to be drawn away from her deep recollection"131.

Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte specifies in greater detail:

"The Servant of God was most observant, indeed most scrupulous in the observance of divine and ecclesiastical law, and words cannot express how much she hated and abhorred sin; rather, she gave every possible and imaginable attention to avoiding even the slightest faults. She never undertook anything without having invoked divine help, and always kept her mind turned toward her God; from this it follows that she was always in continual union with her Good, speaking of him always and with such expressiveness, with such tenderness, as to kindle even the hardest and coldest hearts. Her prayer was continuous, always constant and fervent, until death.

Whenever the Servant of God heard some thoughtless person blaspheme the Holy Name of God, Sister Anna del Salvatore was horrified, even trembling, and would intone aloud "Blessed be God," etc., and, so that no greater offense would be committed against His Divine Majesty, she sought every means to calm the madman and then made reparation for the outrage through exercises of penance and mortification which she inflicted on her already exhausted body. Besides the frequent, that is, continual works of devotion which she kept repeating throughout the day, the Servant of God addressed her Jesus with continual and fiery aspirations"132.

And Sister Anna Maristella Calderone confirms:

"Love for God overflowed warmly in her soul, which often made her break out into expressions, acts, and works that showed the beautiful and great soul she was"133.

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari reports:

"... Her union with God was evident the moment one drew near her: her very bearing, her way of walking, everything proclaimed a soul who had a real intimacy with God; and when need led us to speak to her, she always had Jesus as her example on her lips and in her heart, with the sweetness of counsel and teaching"134.

Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi, who had the Servant of God as her superior in Florence, recalls:

"Being most observant of the law of the Lord, she abhorred sin and sought to avoid even the slightest faults; one could always see in her actions her union with God, of whom she spoke frequently and with fervor, always cheerful; she was heroic in the exercises of prayer; when she heard worldly talk, and, on other occasions, some obscene word or blasphemy, and upon seeing some offense against God, she was grieved; if she could prevent it through her own intervention, she did so, or else resorted to prayer and aspirations such as "My Jesus, mercy, enlighten them and forgive them," etc.; if they were poor, she also gave them alms so that they would stop offending God; many times she said: if it were possible, I would make any sacrifice and penance, provided I were allowed to prevent such a sin"135.

Sister Anna Paolina Viani confirms:

"Her delight was to be at the feet of Jesus in the Sacrament, when her duties and the exercise of charity did not prevent her; and oh, with what fervor she prayed! An offense against God grieved her immensely, and one cannot say what she would not have done to prevent it"136.

And further, in the funeral oration at the solemn obsequies of Sister Anna del Salvatore, Fr. Gaetano Gabriele highlights the charity she had toward God from her youth:

"God went before her with his grace, with his gifts; and she breathes God, speaks of God, consecrates to God the tenderest affections of her heart, the dearest longings of her soul...

She, then, abandoned her parents, her relatives, her homeland; she gave herself wholly to God in the religious family of St. Anne, simply to satisfy the burning longing of her heart: to consecrate herself as the bride of Jesus, and to devote herself to the service of the sick poor"137.

Likewise, in the Report on the charity of the Servant of God, the Historical Experts write as follows:

"Having entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, she continued to progress along this path. Sister Anna Maristella Calderone says of her: 'The chief thought and affection around which the whole life and activity of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore gathered was nothing other than God. Of him she spoke continually with her religious sisters, of him she conversed with the sick she went to assist, on his perfections she meditated, of him she felt the continual presence... Her very actions were interpenetrated with prayer, which never ceased from her lips or from her heart'"138.

Also in the first biography of 1893, written by Onorata Colli at the request of Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno, on this subject, among other things, we read:

"She loved prayer and felt herself especially set aflame for Jesus. When she was in the presence of the Blessed Sacrament, she neither saw nor heard anything of what was happening around her, and, if she had been allowed, she would have remained kneeling at the foot of the altar day and night, taking neither food nor rest"139.

The very goodness of God, acknowledged, adored, loved with an act of total devotion, was the object of the Servant of God's prayer and of her self-offering to the Lord, as a daily gift of love.

Love of neighbor

Charity toward one's neighbor is born of a deep faith, which makes one see God in every brother or sister, especially if poor and suffering, as well as of love toward God, who regards as done to himself what we do for our brothers and sisters.

This virtue is striking in Sister Anna del Salvatore. Hers was a singular charity, affable, ever available, carried out with the whole dedication of her heart and in hiddenness, because wholly supernatural; a single whole with her intimate charity toward God. She truly served her neighbor, especially the sick, without preference, with amiability and motherly care typical of her charism as a Daughter of St. Anne, bringing joy and a smile everywhere, doing good to those who did her harm, lavishing herself wholly on everyone, even to the point of self-forgetfulness and the consummation and immolation of her life.

This love of neighbor is described in detail by all the witnesses, because it is a virtue that shows itself in works.

In the Report of the Experts "in re historica," in this regard we read:

"The commandment of love, pointed out by Jesus as the greatest, together with the love of God, and as a sign by which the world may believe, was lived by Sister Anna del Salvatore with particular overtones toward her religious sisters and toward the people whom, by vocation, she had to assist. Love of neighbor sprang from the awareness of being loved by God, an awareness that filled her with intimate joy; she thus placed herself beside people with attitudes of a typically motherly dedication, drawing her inspiration from Mother St. Anne"140.

- She discovered and adored Jesus in her neighbor.

Charity toward neighbor in Anna del Salvatore has as its theological root the fact that in her brothers and sisters she discovered and adored Jesus; she loved her neighbor in God and for God.

Sister Anna Elisabetta Veronesi wrote:

"One could plainly see that her delight was to serve the sick, in whom she truly recognized the adorable person of Jesus, and she always preferred the poorest"141.

Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi, too, underscores this dimension:

"She loved the poor as the very person of Jesus; indeed, in her care she preferred the poorest and most needy, consoling them with such sweetness that she always left them content and full of admiration; she also brought them alms meant for that purpose, and devotional objects they liked; many times she asked ladies she knew to send the doctor free of charge, and medicines as well; she herself would comb their hair, make their beds, sweep their rooms, etc., and so she urged us to do the same, for what we do for the poor we do for Jesus..."142.

And Sister Anna Paolina Viani:

"She served everyone with equal charity, rich and poor alike, for she was truly convinced that she was serving Jesus in the persons of those sick people"143.

Anna del Salvatore always loved her neighbor as herself, according to the commandment of love (cf. Mt 22:39). This love of service the Servant of God learned from girlhood within the walls of her home, loving and serving her younger siblings whom her mother entrusted to her, besides her other relatives, sacrificing for this even the rightful desire to enjoy herself with girls her own age.

In the Report of the Historical Experts, we read:

"She helped her mother raise her younger siblings not only with material care but also by passing on the religious teachings she herself learned and then pondered in prayer. For some time she was in the service of two priest-uncles, showing kindness and wisdom in managing their respective rectories; moreover, she lovingly looked after and cared for two brothers who attended the Seminary of Bedonia as day students»144.

Fr. Tommaso Grilli, of Albareto, writing in 1913 to the sister of the Servant of God, Sister Anna Fabiana Orsi, said:

"Being the firstborn, she helped her own mother with all care and patience to raise and look after her little brothers and sisters. In this she was certainly always of great relief and benefit through the exercise of her charity"145.

And Orsolina Bottego, writing to Don Valentino Orsi, further specified:

"Orsi, being the firstborn of the family, taught Christian upbringing and doctrine to her dear brothers and accompanied them to the sacrifice of Holy Mass, and raised them in a Christian manner within the holy Catholic Religion"146.

- Charity toward the Sisters of the Congregation

Sister Anna del Salvatore loved her religious sisters tenderly, and whenever she saw one of them sad or afflicted, whether from homesickness or for some other reason, she solicitously sought to cheer and encourage her, speaking to her of the comfort she would receive in serving Jesus, in suffering for him.

To drive away sadness, she would invite them to prayer, and was altogether happy when she saw the smile and the peace of heart return to them.

In the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, the memory of the motherly love that Sister Anna del Salvatore showed toward all the Sisters, both spiritually and materially, is still very much alive.

In the depositions of the Ordinary Process of Palermo, all the eyewitnesses speak of the extraordinary and heroic charity exercised by Sister Anna del Salvatore, always and toward everyone.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, speaking of charity toward neighbor, describes very well Sister Anna del Salvatore's love for her Sisters, and her care and concern for their spiritual health. Among other things, he states:

"As to charity toward neighbor, I distinguish between charity of a spiritual order and charity of a bodily order. As to the first, much could be said; but I recall that once, obliged by obedience to accompany a Sister from Palermo to Trapani, she went, even though she was running a very high fever: she then brought her back to Palermo, nor would she leave her there, for fear that some spiritual harm might come to her. This was told to me by the Sister herself, named Sister Anna M. Grazia, who added that Sister Anna del Salvatore had reached the station to return to Palermo, and from there, as though inspired, she went back to the house, saying: no, I will not leave her at all. In general, I can say that she had great zeal for souls, and spared neither effort nor suffering so long as she could do good to souls. As to the body, one could not finish praising her: she was always ready to keep vigil in attending the sick, and also to spare the Sisters. It is also well known, and I always heard it said, how she would rise at night to do the Sisters' laundry, to spare those who would otherwise have had to do it. This seemed a remarkable thing, because it was impossible that so much work could be done in a single night; so that those who were obliged to go to the laundry at the appointed hour, that is, very early, found, to their astonishment, everything already done. I also recall that once, perhaps in winter, having arrived in Palermo at a late hour, having climbed the stairs of the house, so as not to disturb the Sisters, she remained outside after having knocked lightly and not been heard, and this because the Sisters had not been told beforehand of her arrival. She herself chose for herself the sick who were most repulsive, whether from sores or for some other reason; and the sick preferred to be attended or treated by her, because she had a quite special way of treating them, which I do not know how to account for"147.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, asserts:

"... what she did for her religious Sisters, comforting, helping, and relieving them, I know for certain personally.

I have heard of how much the Servant of God did on behalf of young women, whether at risk or poor, and of the zeal she had for their well-being.

It is true what is said... of her self-abnegation in caring for the sick, even the most filthy and wretched.

... the Servant of God was animated by this spirit of sacrifice for the good of her neighbors.

As to her evenness of spirit toward her neighbors, by which she made no distinctions of persons, I know this for certain and attest to it"148.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, assures:

"Her charity toward the Sisters was immense; she helped them, sympathized with them, encouraged them to sacrifice. She loved to go to the aid of the sick, especially the poorest"149.

Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, specifies:

"... preferring especially the homes of the poor, considering herself most happy to go to these houses: and this, too, I know personally."150

Fr. Giuseppe Palazzotto, the fifth witness, confirms:

"As to charity toward neighbor, I can say and attest that she was wholly given to everyone, sparing nothing of herself, both toward the Sisters, with whom she behaved like a true mother, and in caring for the sick at home, hastening with great love to fulfill this pious office"151.

"... She was so zealous for the good of her neighbor that, though suffering and exhausted of strength, she would surpass herself, going to care for the sick"152.

Sister Anna Serafina Gregory, too, the sixth witness, maintains:

"... she was a flame of charity, and that love which burned in her breast for God impelled her toward her suffering neighbor: and so she would hasten, ready and cheerful, to care for the sick, who, as was said, always wanted her; for it was said that when she came, they suffered less"153.

In the Servant of God's correspondence we find continual confirmation of the solicitude and love she bore toward all the sisters entrusted to her by the Foundress Mother, to whom she reported punctually on the state of the Community and of each individual sister.

For their spiritual good she was attentive in choosing ordinary and extraordinary confessors. Writing to the Foundress Mother on 29 March 1877, on this subject, she says:

"Dear Mother, we have the extraordinary [confessor] and he is so good, but he is a Missionary; the sisters are all happy... If you think it good to keep him, then I shall go to the Archbishop and have him left to us"154.

When she then writes to individual sisters, she addresses each with true affection, informs her of everything concerning the Institute, shares spiritual experiences, and expresses to all her feelings of kindness and concern for their good. She also always asks for news of the other sisters she has known, and promises them her prayers155.

The Historical Experts express themselves thus in their report:

"As a simple sister and as a superior, the feelings of esteem and benevolence she bore toward her religious sisters led her to be attentive to their needs and to anticipate them, showing on every occasion a truly motherly delicacy... She sought in every way to lighten the sisters' burdens by performing herself the heaviest tasks of the House. Sister Anna Gregoria Poppelmann states: '[she was] all heart and charity toward those under her, whom she loved as a tender mother, and she knew how to draw honey even from bitter flowers. And what shall be said of her charity toward the sick sisters? These were her favorite portion'"156.

In the trial testimonies de auditu a videntibus as well, the immense and profound charity of the Servant of God is highlighted.

- Charity toward the sick, the poor, and the weakest.

Imbued with the charism of her Congregation, the Servant of God devoted herself with joy and with a true spirit of Christian charity and motherly dedication to the care of the sick and the poor. She was not frightened by the squalor and misery of the hovels she had to visit in order to tend the sick. She desired especially to care for those sick who caused the most revulsion, and with love and infinite patience she rendered to those unfortunate people every necessary service.

The Servant of God cared for the whole person: soul and body, for she was aware that through the body it was easier to reach and heal the soul as well. During the care she gave, with consoling words, she exhorted the sick to resignation, to patience, to the love of God.

Sister Anna Margherita Tripi, the first witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, deposes in this regard:

"... the characteristic note of the Servant of God's spirituality is to be found in her generous charity toward the poor"157.

Sister Anna Vincenza Lo Bue, the fourth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, confirms:

"... the Servant of God exercised charity in the service of the sick and the poor in keeping with the Foundress's principal idea, and almost in keeping with the spirit of charity of the Bocconiste Sisters, founded by Blessed Giacomo Cusmano, with whom she was initially lodged in Palermo"158.

Sister Anna Carmela Lo Baido, the sixth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, declares herself convinced that:

"... the Servant of God, especially in Sicily, where she was sent as Provincial Superior, faithfully carried out what our Foundress desired, devoting herself with great and generous charity to the service of the sick at home and of the poor"159.

Sister Vincenzina Scalzo, the sixteenth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, attests:

"... the Servant of God was most distinguished for her expressions of charity for the benefit of the community and of the people who came near her"160.

Likewise, in the documents appended to the Cause, it is evident how the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore exercised the theological virtue of charity toward neighbor in a truly heroic way.

In the report of the Historical Experts, indeed, we read:

"... Her work as a nurse brought to light her capacity to care for those who suffered, among whom she always chose the poorest and those afflicted with repulsive diseases..."161.

Thus, in her report, Sister Anna Nazaria Provera makes known:

"She loved the poor, helping them in all their needs. She was solicitous toward the sick poor, spending whole nights lavishing on them all the care their infirmities required. She softened their sufferings with the most gracious manner, to such a degree that word went around that she was a great Saint. All the sick wished to be cared for by her, for the relief they felt"162.

And Sister Anna Costanza Cenni further asserts:

"Her spirit of sacrifice reached the point of heroism; she would have suffered any pain to see her neighbor happy in every respect"163.

Likewise, Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte attests:

"The Servant of God was all love and charity toward the poor, especially when sick; she helped them generously as far as her strength allowed, comforted them, and then commended them to the rich so that they might relieve them. Immense was the charity she had toward the sick who were poor and abandoned, especially those with contagious diseases. The Servant of God cared for them with love and charity, cleaned them, dressed their putrid and gangrenous sores, urged them to have patience and resignation, and led them to regard their bed as the Cross of Jesus; she had them go to confession and communion, and prepared them for the great passage. She was tireless with poor, obstinate sinners; she left no means untried to convert them and draw them to God. She used the most winning ways to induce them to abandon sin; she made them promises of generous gifts, if they were poor; and when that was not enough, she resorted to prayer and penance, chastising her own body and mistreating it with fasts, hairshirts, and harsh and bloody disciplines. She used this same practice of penances to assist the holy Souls in Purgatory. She always prayed for her enemies, especially for her most relentless persecutors, and never uttered the slightest complaint against them"164.

Sister Anna Irene Carmeli reveals:

"... Sister Anna del Salvatore also practiced charity toward all those in need in general, but was most sensitive toward the sick Sisters, seeing to it that they lacked nothing necessary, caring for them herself, and comforting them to suffer in order to gain merit for paradise"165.

Sister Anna Raffaela Ceruti reveals:

"Her charity toward neighbor was limitless, especially in caring for the sick at home: she was always the first, day and night, not disdaining to render the humblest services, especially to the poor who lacked necessities, and it was there that her charity shone most, begging alms from the rich to relieve the misery of others.

With the Sisters, her charity stood out even more, relieving them of their burdens, taking upon herself the heaviest ones; with the sick she exercised the utmost vigilance that they be provided with everything that could help relieve them, both morally, with charitable words, urging them to suffer everything for the love of God, who suffered so much for us, and physically, making sure nothing was lacking for that purpose"166.

Sister Anna Maristella Calderone specifies:

"She also greatly loved her neighbor in God and for God. There was no class of people she forgot, no physical or moral misery she did not soften; there was no sacrifice, even a heroic one, to which she would not submit, provided she could dry a tear and console someone unhappy"167.

The poor, then, had her special predilection: she loved them with motherly love and lavished on them the most delicate and affectionate care. With pleasure she lingered with them, instructed them, sought to help them by every means, even going to knock on the doors of the rich and of benefactors to obtain some help.

We read what Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari states:

"The poor! They were indeed the person of Christ for our heroine; on them she lavished her care with the fervor of one who wishes to please her beloved, to them her pure and comforting smiles, to them her caresses and the cheerful help that never humiliated, and all ran to her, both the needy and the afflicted, and found, as each needed, bodily comfort, the soul's relief when, oppressed by anguish, they went to pour it out upon that heart which, understanding them, shared the sorrows of poor mortals, and knew how to dry their bitter tears, lifting hearts to God. To the rich she bound the cause of the poor, whenever she herself could not supply all their needs, making them understand the lofty Mission God had given them on earth, making them treasurers for the poor.

For the sick she had, moreover, a vocation of love: to them she gave her labor with that ardor which perceives the good, exalts it, makes it beautiful. For the poorest she had the greater predilection, and she never failed to join to bodily comfort the strength of spirit that is so often lost in the great moment of passing. Then, like a true athlete, she offered her fortitude to the souls in need, and with the good Spirit she ministered the sweetness of the life to come, thus sharpening, in the soul that shortly before had perhaps greatly feared that God the judge, the desire for rest in the bosom of God in the face of its earthly end"168.

In the biography concerning Sister Anna del Salvatore, Roberta Cecilia Frati writes:

"Her skill and delicacy in tending the sick, her ability to instill confidence and serenity, her preference for the poorest sick and for those with repulsive diseases, make her a much-appreciated nurse, and all the sick who knew her or heard of her wished her at the bedside of their suffering"169.

Practicing charity universally, without distinctions, the Servant of God never allowed herself a judgment of condemnation toward anyone, not even toward those who might possibly have been against her. She always took greatly to heart the esteem due to every person. For this reason she was never heard to speak ill of others; rather, she always sought to excuse their faults.

"I never heard from the lips of the Servant of God," attests Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, "a single word that could offend charity toward neighbor"170.

"She never complained, whatever injury she received. I myself observed," states Sister Anna Nazaria Provera, "that, having received a grave injury, she trembled from the effort she made upon herself, yet did not utter a single word in her own defense"171.

And Sister Anna Paolina Viani confirms:

"She loved everyone with equal affection; when offended, when slandered, she forgave generously and prayed for those who offended her"172.

From all that has been said and reported, we can affirm with assurance that the charity of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore never failed in any circumstance or before any difficulty; rather, it kept growing.

Her love for God, which was her life and for which she longed with all her heart, was immense. She had a charity extended to every kind of person, without the slightest distinction: she received everyone affably and loved everyone in the same way, for in everyone she saw, loved, and served God.

From this synthesis of the theological virtues of Sister Anna del Salvatore, and from all that can further be gathered from an attentive reading, especially of the statements and reports of people close to her or who have studied and admired her life and actions, we can form a sure conviction of the high spiritual quality of her conduct, and of the number of people reached by her so far-reaching service of charity.

Everything she did and everything she bore in order to please God (cf. 1 Pet 2:20), for her life was "abscondita cum Christo in Deo" [hidden with Christ in God] (Col 3:3).

Up to this point an effort has been made to prove, on the basis of the trial testimonies and the witnesses' reports, that the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore exercised in heroic degree the theological virtues of faith, hope, and charity toward God and toward her neighbor.

Now, the Christian who believes, hopes, and loves lives the dimension of the person in fullness. Even if with effort, in keeping with his temperament and upbringing, he exercises the cardinal virtues with heroism.

"These virtues group together all the others and are the hinges of a virtuous life. They are: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

Human virtues are stable dispositions of the intellect and the will that govern our acts, order our passions, and guide our conduct according to reason and faith. Acquired and strengthened by repeated morally good acts, they are purified and elevated by divine grace" (Compendium of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, 378-379).

Without the practice of these virtues, the theological virtues would be mere appearance, as Sacred Scripture says: "If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees cannot love God whom he does not see... whoever loves God must also love his brother" (cf. 1 Jn 4:20-21); and "as the body without the spirit is dead, so also faith without works is dead" (Jas 2:26).

The sanctity of the Servant of God is therefore also proved through the prompt, constant, and joyful observance of the cardinal virtues, and we shall show below how Sister Anna del Salvatore practiced them heroically.

a) Heroic Prudence

"Prudence is the virtue that disposes practical reason to discern our true good in every circumstance and to choose the right means of achieving it... It is called auriga virtutum — charioteer of the virtues: it guides the other virtues by setting rule and measure for them" (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1806). According to St. Thomas, prudence is the virtue most necessary for human life; indeed, it is proper to prudence to apply and spread, through the maze of concrete life, the law of morality and conformity to the will of God, in which the perfection of man consists.

Heroic prudence is to be understood as the moral virtue that directs all human actions according to right reason and makes it possible to live in full accord with the mind of the Gospel; for this reason it holds first place among the other cardinal virtues.

The Servant of God possessed an admirable prudence joined to a holy simplicity. This virtue showed itself throughout her life, for she always had as her end, in each of her actions, the Glory of God and the attainment of eternal Beatitude, making use of every fitting and suitable means to reach it.

From her youth, and later also in religious life as a Daughter of St. Anne, she sought in prayer the light to know the will of God, and always asked advice from whoever directed her conscience.

Already in the Novitiate, Sister Anna del Salvatore's prudence appeared splendidly, so that she was soon entrusted with the office of Superior in a newly founded house; and she was admired by all who knew her for her great prudence in carrying out the many duties entrusted to her. The esteem the Foundress Mother and her Council held for the Servant of God grew ever greater, to the point of appointing her, only a few years later, Provincial Superior of all the communities of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily.

In the exercise of this virtue, the Servant of God gave clear proof of balance, wisdom, discretion, and shrewdness, and was never hasty or attached to her own views, but constantly resorted to reflection, prayer, and the counsel of others, even when she could perfectly well have chosen and guided herself alone. This showed itself clearly in all the houses where Sister Anna del Salvatore lived or carried out her mission, helping her Sisters to overcome various difficulties through her judgments and her counsel.

The second Theological Censor, in this regard, writes:

"The numerous difficulties and trials she encountered are all borne and resolved in the long hours of adoration before the Sacrament, which instill in her courage and optimism"173.

And further:

"Never does she show full confidence in her own judgment or in her own conduct, but always submits everything to the judgment of the Foundress"174.

His Excellency Msgr. Zuccaro, the first witness, affirms:

"She was prudent in governing the Community as a simple Superior of the House of the nurses, and then much more so when, as Provincial Superior, she governed all the houses of Sicily"175.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, too, the third witness, maintains in this regard:

"Her prudence was revealed in directing the Community, so that they all lived in unbroken peace"176.

"The Servant of God exercised this virtue and always studied ways to succeed in things, even difficult ones"177.

All the documents and the witnesses' statements in the Process agree in presenting Sister Anna del Salvatore as a true model of a Sister and Superior, full of evangelical wisdom and good judgment, capable of listening, humble, ready to guide and encourage the Communities, discreet yet decisive in establishing relations with ecclesiastical and civil authorities.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, attests in this regard:

"In the time I knew her, I can attest that, on many occasions, she gave many proofs of an admirable prudence.

This prudence in her choice of the religious state speaks for itself.

... that the Servant of God was sent to govern various Houses, as proof of the prudence of the Servant of God, seems an evident thing.

... the Servant of God was appointed Provincial of all the houses of Sicily at the General Chapter: this shows the trust all the Chapter members had in her.

This trust the administrators had in her prudence in the various Houses is also known to me personally.

It is true, and I know, of this spirit of counsel of hers, through which the Sisters received direction and comfort from her"178.

Sister Anna Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, observes:

"This is gathered from the effects, that is, from having chosen the religious state in order to acquire greater perfection"179.

Sister Anna Serafina Gregory, the sixth witness, specifies:

"... I heard it said that the Servant of God governed the Community with great prudence and charity, so that all the Sisters esteemed her and regarded her as a Saint"180.

Sister Anna Margherita Tripi, the first witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, is convinced that

"... the particular and principal activity carried out by the Servant of God was that of her provincial superiorship in Sicily, which she took up with great responsibility, and which was appreciated by superiors and faithful alike, so much so that she, the Servant of God, was called the 'little Saint of Palermo' ('Santuzza di Palermo')"181.

Sister Anna Irene Cadoni, the eighth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, emphasizes:

"As to her spirituality, I would point to poverty, prudence, simplicity, and industriousness. She relieved her Sisters of work and sacrificed herself for them. The Servant of God could offer people today the example of the above-mentioned virtues"182.

The letters of the Servant of God, especially those to the Foundress Mother Blessed Rosa Gattorno, offer a complete picture of Sister Anna del Salvatore's virtue of prudence: she reports every smallest detail of how her work was progressing, always asks advice and authorization for every smallest matter, and continually reports on the houses where she was Superior.

"Mother, they have suggested I go visit the mayor and the secretary, because the hospital is finished; should I go or not... Mother... I will do as you say"183.

"Yesterday two [girls] came: one would pay 20 lire and is twelve and a half years old, and the other, who would pay 15, is eight years old. Dear Mother, I beg you to tell me whether I should accept them or not; then I beg you, if you can, to tell me how I should conduct myself regarding Sister Anna Anastasia about the baths"184.

Many are the requests for help addressed to the Servant of God, and she always asks the Foundress Mother's advice about them:

"Princess Strozzi came, gave me 20 lire, and then told me she had thought of giving the direction of these blind people to nuns, and so had thought of taking the Daughters of St. Anne, because she considers them more suited, and that for now she would need three, and afterward hoped to increase this pious work. Then she left it to me to let her know something soon..."185.

"Then I would like to ask you whether you can give me permission to send the two girls of Fossi to the vigil [they are two boarding pupils]... You cannot believe the entreaties they make me, they even kneel down... Believe me, dear Mother, that many times I cannot hold out... So, if you allow me, I will send them sometimes"186.

Sister Anna Nazaria Provera writes:

"In all her way of acting she was most prudent. She had no other aim than the Glory of God. She did nothing without the counsel of the Spiritual Director and of the dear Mother, toward whom she felt deep veneration. At a sign from her, she would undertake any journey, with no regard for fatigue. At home everything went forward in order. She was the first at the hardest work, especially the laundry, by night and by day"187.

From the report of Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte, too, we learn:

"The prudence the Servant of God practiced was quite different from that of worldly people; for her actions were wholly directed toward God, from whom she expected to obtain eternal glory. And she sought to attain it with an irreproachable purity of conscience; hence she had a great fear of offending God; hence prayer was continual in her, as was the scrupulous watchfulness over her senses, subjecting her rebellious flesh to the spirit through never-interrupted disciplines, hairshirts, fasts, and mortifications of every kind. All this she carried out with order and with the express obedience of her superiors and spiritual directors, toward whom she bore an untouchable respect and veneration"188.

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari reports:

"Of our Sister's heroic Prudence I can affirm that she showed continual self-abnegation; she never looked to herself, so as to hasten wherever her work was needed, and, at the cost of any sacrifice, she was ready to relieve every physical or moral pain: and so, always solicitous for the good of her neighbor, for the growth of the Institute, intent only on diligent activity, she fled idleness, thus showing herself a model of virtue and of work"189.

And Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi confirms in her report:

"Her prudence was truly for the Lord, and the sole aim of all her actions was to attain eternal glory; her life was a continual work and prayer, the enemy of idleness; indeed she spent nights to spare the sisters and gain merit in secret, washing the dirtiest linen and pumping the water for the wash, which in the morning was already found done, although she was of most afflicted health"190.

In the choice of her vocation too — as already noted — Sister Anna del Salvatore did not decide rashly, but let herself be guided by a supernatural prudence. She insistently asked for the Lord's help, submitted herself to the counsel of those who could rightly guide her, and awaited the approval of her family as well, which, though at first showing itself opposed, later granted her every support for her vocation among the Daughters of St. Anne191.

But the exemplary character of her practice of this virtue shone forth even more, especially in the most difficult and delicate circumstances of our Servant of God's whole life, in which, acting according to the particular interior light received in prayer, or the counsel of the Foundress Mother, or the direction of her spiritual Directors, she always knew how to choose what leads to acquiring or increasing the true wealth: the love of God.

b) Heroic Justice

St. Thomas, as with every other virtue, holds justice to be a "habit," that is, a habitual disposition of the soul, which tends to give each person his due. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (no. 1807) defines the virtue of justice thus:

"Justice is the moral virtue that consists in the constant and firm will to give God and neighbor their due."

Through it, then, we understand and consequently do what is good toward God, toward ourselves, and toward our neighbor. As a moral virtue, justice is a gift of God's grace that develops and is perfected in the school of the Word (cf. Psalms 111; 118:1-8). Justice thus refers precisely to that supernatural habit which constantly inclines the Christian to do good by giving to each what belongs to him. Sacred Scripture links it with holiness (Mt 5:6).

Through such a virtue — which demands, above all, love — the Christian shares in the holiness of God, to whom he will relate at every moment and always, for "in him we live and move and have our being" (Acts 17:28). One is thus held to be just who, living by faith, carries out the will of God with candor and constancy, and strives for the common good.

Sister Anna del Salvatore had precisely this "habit" of justice. The first manifestation of her heroic practice of the virtue of justice toward God was her aspiration always to seek greater perfection, doing only and always the will of God and rendering to him the honor due him. For this reason she always made sure, with the utmost care, that everything concerning his worship was in order in the Church. Moreover, she never ceased to thank the Lord for having had her born within the bosom of the Church and for the grace of having called her to the religious state.

The Servant of God practiced the virtue of justice in heroic degree, rendering to everyone, according to their station, the honor and respect due them. Moreover, she was always obedient and respectful toward her Superiors.

The observance of the virtue of justice toward her neighbor led Sister Anna del Salvatore never to deceive anyone and never to deny anyone what was owed to them, so that in every one of her daily acts she conveyed this strong sense of justice to all those around her.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, declares:

"I can attest, both from having heard it said and from my own experience, that the Servant of God was most observant not only of what concerns the law of God and the Precepts of the Church, but also of the duties and rules of the holy Institute"192.

"The Servant of God was grateful to the Lord and always thanked him, not only for the vocation to the faith, but also for the vocation to the religious state"193.

"... she had great zeal for the decorum of the House of God, both for the decent cleanliness of the Church and the Sacred furnishings, and also for the composure she wanted kept in the Church"194.

"... the Servant of God never harmed anyone, either by failing in truth or by failing in justice, that is, in the interest of others"195.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, attests:

"Christian justice was for her like a special virtue, giving to God what was God's and to her Neighbor what was her Neighbor's"196.

Sister Anna Carmela Lo Baido, the sixth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, specifies:

"... the Servant of God, especially in Sicily, where she was sent as Provincial Superior, faithfully carried out what our Foundress desired, devoting herself with great and generous charity to the service of the sick at home and of the poor"197.

The first Theological Censor writes:

"From reading the letters there emerges immediately, and with impressive constancy, a clear and open character... This personality trait is evident in her serene outlook on daily life and can be observed more closely in her unconditional acceptance of the duties of her state, especially in the boundless sensitivity shown toward the Institute to which she belonged and its Rule, toward the other sisters entrusted to her, toward the Foundress Mother, toward the sick, poor and rich alike, toward benefactors and other figures who passed through the scene of her mission (for example, priests and bishops)"198.

The second Theological Censor observes:

"Through her constancy in the exercise of the virtues and in fulfilling the duties of her state, with the responsibilities entrusted to her, the Servant of God shows to what degree she assimilated the spirit of the Institute, in the meticulous observance of the Rule and in unconditional obedience to the Foundress and to her direct Superiors. The testimony of her solicitude in living out that spirit, especially in caring for the sick and in fidelity to the Rule, down to a few days before her death, though already gravely ill, shows the heroic endurance of this woman, who tirelessly sought to obey and thereby to follow the divine will"199.

Sister Anna del Salvatore practiced the virtue of justice by faithfully attending to all her duties. Writing from Florence to the Foundress Mother, believing she had failed in her duty by causing disorder in the Community, she says:

"Oh God, what sorrow, what great pain it was for me to hear that in this community there is so much disorder because of me. My God, what heartbreak... Ah, my dear Mother, if this happens through my fault, you, so good, may remove me so as not to give this scandal, and then this holy community will flourish and spread its most beautiful branches throughout this beautiful city; however, I am ready to do in everything and for everything whatever you command me, and, if I had to remain my whole life long in this community, I would gladly do so, provided my dear Mother is content..."200.

And in another letter, also to the Foundress Mother, dated 21 February 1878, she writes thus:

"Dear Mother, I assure you that even had you not obliged me by obedience, I would have told you the plain truth... Dear Mother, I may have erred, but with you, my beloved Mother, I came with the plain truth"201.

From the reports of the Sisters, her religious companions, we learn that the Servant of God took care never to tell the smallest lie and — as already said — observed justice toward her neighbor, never deceiving anyone in any way. Likewise, there emerged in her the absence of any form of favoritism toward persons, a point on which she was very demanding.

In the report of Sister Anna Del Consiglio Chiaramonte we read:

"The Servant of God was most zealous for everything concerning the worship of God. She was submissive, obedient, and respectful toward her Superiors to the point of scrupulousness, humble and gentle with her equals, trustworthy and charitable with the sick, and the same toward everyone. Her words and her speech were simple, without even a hint of pretense, duplicity, or dissimulation"202.

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari likewise reports:

"Toward her Superiors she showed the respectful submission of one humble who sees herself raised to high office solely by another's kindness; faithful to their wishes, she wanted everyone to find the yoke sweet; toward those under her she was, more than a Superior, a Mother in the dealings of her office, which knew no commanding, and in her humility she held herself inferior to the very Sisters she governed. And of her it could truly be said that she had no place to seek rest in the hours that follow the weariness of long labors; and, while she took care that the Sisters lacked nothing, she allowed herself to lack a bed, a nightstand — in short, the necessities. Never in my sight could she be accused of duplicity or pretense in her conduct, but, simple in word as in deed, she treated us as a good Sister who lives on love and, with its rays, kindly lights up all around her"203.

And Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi confirms:

"Most zealous for everything concerning the worship of God, most humble and ready at any sign from her superiors, provided there was not the slightest offense against charity..."204.

c) Heroic Fortitude

The virtue of fortitude, before being a special virtue, is a general disposition of firmness, a condition necessary for the exercise of every virtue. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (no. 1808) defines it thus:

"Fortitude is the moral virtue that ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good. It strengthens the resolve to resist temptations and to overcome obstacles in the moral life."

The Servant of God Anna del Salvatore was endowed with an admirable fortitude and exercised it in heroic degree both in undertaking difficult situations and in bearing adversities, advancing and courageously overcoming every obstacle that arose in the course of her life. One is indeed struck to see how, in her constant and most faithful practice of this virtue, she was able to carry out her daily duty without pause, without wavering, always sustained by a great love for God.

In this regard, His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro affirms:

"This virtue accompanied her in all the acts of her life, not only in the exercise of the virtues, but also in adversities and persecutions, until death"205.

She showed this virtue from her youth, within her family. In every circumstance she showed herself good and affectionate, seeking to relieve the sufferings and hardships of her family, caused by economic want, through love and diligence in work, always keeping her good humor and serenity. The first biographer of the Servant of God, in 1893, describes the care Sister Anna del Salvatore took of her little brothers and sisters. Her mother, occupied with other work, entrusted them entirely to her.

"With what love she watched over them! With what self-denial she gave up enjoying herself with other girls her own age, in order to stay with them! How patient she was in bearing their whims, and how eager she showed herself to satisfy their legitimate wishes!"206.

With great fortitude of spirit, she sacrificed herself to follow her two brothers, admitted as day students to the seminary of Bedonia:

"Marianna had to follow them there to prepare their food, look after the laundry, attend to the cleaning of the house, and guide them"207.

From the biographies and testimonies we learn of the sad economic situation of the Orsi family:

"The family's financial conditions, meanwhile, change. The growing number of children and new needs lead Angelo Mussi to incur debts, to pay off which he is forced, in 1862, to sell his properties and move to Centovera, in the Piacenza area.

Marianna remains in Albareto with her uncle, the mayor Lorenzo Mussi, then rejoins the family, which now, more than ever, needs her.

In Centovera, life for the Orsi family is not easy, and hardships are keenly felt.

To help her parents with a little extra income, Marianna goes to work in the service of the Bottego family, a family originally from Albareto..."208.

But our Servant of God

"showing herself on every occasion a good, affectionate, and submissive daughter, she sought to relieve the sufferings of her family with love, diligence in work, and by keeping a cheerful mood at home, even when the straits in which they lived might have made her shed bitter tears. Inwardly, however, she was troubled at the thought that her father, her mother, and her brothers were in distress... Most fervent, therefore, were the prayers she raised to God, that he might improve her family's circumstances"209.

For all this, she showed great fortitude when she had to part from her family to follow her religious vocation. The family, though God-fearing, needed her, needed her help, so that at first they were displeased with Marianna's decision to enter a religious Institute. So many and so fervent, however, were her prayers to the Lord that in the end she obtained the desired consent210.

The Servant of God, now resolved to follow her vocation, also had to suffer inwardly. With true supernatural fortitude, however, she also overcame the tremendous struggles to which the devil subjected her, tempting her in a thousand ways. The first biographer writes:

"As with all chosen souls, the minister of evil showed himself under various guises, and the poor girl was not spared the most frightful temptations. Now it was the thought of her parents, from whose support her work had removed one means of livelihood, that urged her to return home; now it was her friends, left behind in her village, who appeared before her gay and cheerful, to lead her back to the free life of the countryside; now it was the doubt of not being able afterward to fulfill all the obligations of her state, which left her uncertain, hesitant; and now she grew afraid at the thought of eternal damnation, which she would deserve by not doing the much — indeed the too much — that monastic life would demand of her"211.

Steadfast in her will, the Servant of God overcame and won these battles, certain that the grace of God was with her, and for this reason she invoked it in her assiduous prayer and from it obtained the strength needed to emerge victorious.

She never let show what she suffered, neither to her superiors nor to the sisters, but was always cheerful and serene.

From Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness of the Process of Palermo, we learn:

"Her whole life is woven through with the spirit of fortitude amid adversities in a truly extraordinary way, although she seemed cheerful and content. I have heard it said that the Servant of God suffered scorn and ill-treatment, not here, but in Florence, where she suffered grave insults and outrages, even being driven off with thrown stones when she went begging"212.

Within her own Institute as well, the Servant of God had much to suffer, and with fortitude she faced reproaches and ill-treatment precisely because of her zeal, her commitment of charity toward her neighbor, and for the good of the Institute itself; reproaches and ill-treatment that were later recognized as unjust, so that she was greatly admired by all her Sisters for the example of goodness she never tired of giving to everyone.

Sister Anna Elisa Scrò, the second witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, declares:

"The way the Servant of God behaved in the most dramatic moments of her life seems to me heroic. She was, in fact, strongly slandered by her religious sisters before the Foundress, who, as a punishment, was about to take away her veil. On that occasion, the Servant of God, feeling herself strongly and wholly bound to God, replied to the Foundress: 'I received the veil before the altar, and if you wish, I will return it before the altar'"213.

And Mr. Pietro Spanò, the twenty-first witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, observes:

"What strikes me most about the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi is her humility and her unconditional dedication to others, particularly to the needy and the suffering, as well as her profound sense of endurance and submission before the adversities of her existence"214.

Reading the Servant of God's correspondence, especially the letters exchanged with the Blessed Foundress, one can clearly see the true Christian fortitude lived out by Sister Anna del Salvatore.

Wherever obedience sent her, she had to bear immense difficulties in establishing new houses, organizing the work, facing ecclesiastical and civil Superiors, and overcoming poverty and privation.

We read in the Report of the Historical Experts:

"The Servant of God faced everything with humble serenity and great strength of spirit, submitting herself completely to the Foundress's judgment"215.

Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte, emphasizing the heroic way in which the Servant of God lived the virtue of fortitude, affirms:

"The Servant of God was always strong in bearing every adversity, both in illness and in the insults and persecutions that came to her through evil people. She was always strong, constant, and undaunted on the path of perfection she had undertaken, showing herself, therefore, always the same both in adverse and in favorable circumstances"216.

From Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari we know that

"... for her everything was little when it concerned her body's discomfort, and, always unchanged, scorning the evil... she carried out with the same strength the most exhausting tasks, to which, with a saint's delight, she submitted with love"217.

Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi, too, emphasizes that the Servant of God was:

"Most strong in bearing adversities and illnesses; indeed, though sick, if her superiors' obedience required it, she would even rise from bed, saying: God commands me and I must obey; courageous on the path of the Lord, she showed herself always the same both in adverse and in favorable circumstances"218.

And Sister Anna Paolina Viani testifies:

"She suffered from physical ills that tormented her, with unfailing patience, saying nothing; we noticed her sufferings by the change of color in her face, but from her one never learned anything; she was always in a cheerful mood"219.

The Servant of God showed the whole of her fortitude of spirit especially in facing and bearing the sufferings of her final illness and in her tranquility as death drew near, despite her young age of 43, herself consoling her Sisters.

Here is what she writes to Blessed Rosa Gattorno on 27 May 1885:

"Having been gravely ill for more than a month, I have never been able to write to you, and now tormented as before by the same pains, which leave me neither by day nor by night and do not allow me, to my great regret, to fulfill those obligations I am bound to, that is, to give you, my good Mother, an account of everything presently happening.

But I assure you that, as soon as I can hold a pen in my hand, I will not fail to give you a full account. I thank you, too, for the concern you show for me and for the prayer you offer to God for my poor health; I beg you to continue it, out of charity, for I have great need of it"220.

And among the eyewitnesses, His Excellency Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro (the first witness), Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi (the second witness), and Sister Anna Serafina Gregory (the sixth witness) attest:

"Despite her outward composure, a deep suffering of spirit showed through in the Servant of God.

I confirm the state of calm that the Servant of God kept at the extremity of her life"221.

"Having been present at the final illness and death of the Servant of God, her patience and fortitude aroused the admiration of all who attended her, myself included"222.

"I can attest that, having gone with Sister Anna Teresa Patti to visit the Servant of God on her deathbed, we found her greatly suffering, yet cheerful and content to die, longing to be united with the Lord"223.

Finally, we wish to sum up the fortitude of the Servant of God with the words of Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness:

"Fortitude seemed in her a kind of paradox, for one could not explain how, in a person so unassuming and humble, there could dwell a heart unalterably strong and resistant to all the difficulties that stood in the way of the exercise of her virtues and her office as Superior"224.

In the exercise of the virtue of fortitude, Sister Anna del Salvatore was certainly guided by love for the Lord and by trust in his sure help, strengthened also by the Gospel's exhortations: "In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage, I have overcome the world" (Jn 16:33), a certainty that allowed her to live out, with her life and in her life, the verse of Psalm 118:14: "The Lord is my strength and my song."

d) Heroic Temperance

"Temperance is the moral virtue that moderates the attraction of pleasures and provides balance in the use of created goods. It ensures the will's mastery over instincts and keeps desires within the limits of what is honorable" (Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1809).

"The temperate man," Pope John Paul II said on 22 November 1978, "is one who is master of himself. One in whom the passions do not get the upper hand over reason, over the will, and over the heart as well. He is the man who knows how to master himself."

With the virtue of temperance, the Christian, enlightened by faith, maintains the right and proper balance toward sensible pleasures. It is one of the most important cardinal virtues in the moral life, because it moderates natural instincts and passions, keeping their exercise within the bounds of reason and faith. Temperance is the source of sobriety and mortification.

The Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore was a most faithful follower of Jesus the Master, including in the need to take up the Cross daily to follow him and become like him. Imbued with this conviction, she exercised the virtue of temperance constantly and heroically from her earliest childhood. As with all the other virtues, family life was for her a true school of temperance.

"... Marianna was much loved throughout the village for the rare gifts with which she was endowed. She had a most gentle temperament and a calm spirit; she was without vanity in dress and bearing; she knew nothing of pretense, and, though she enjoyed being in cheerful company with girls her own age, she was most reserved in her conduct, and in conversation never let slip an improper word"225.

"Clothing everything in amiability and naturalness," states Sister Roberta Cecilia Frati, "she takes on a style of austerity and mortification, both in food and in other aspects of her simple Christian life"226.

Having entered religious life, the Servant of God was even more austere in her diet, eating once a day, feeding on poor and inferior food. She was likewise temperate in her rest. Having spent the day in work and the night in caring for the sick, she never went to rest, maintaining that she felt no need of it, and spending whole nights in prayer. Toward all the other sisters, by contrast, she was solicitous.

Sister Anna del Salvatore never owned a bed, and, considering it a luxury, she always said: "If I were to fall ill, I would indeed find some kind sister who would give up her bed to me; but while, thank God, I enjoy excellent health, here is my bed" — pointing to a chair — "it serves me wonderfully!"

Indulgent, compassionate, solicitous, and full of consideration for her Sisters regarding food, rest, and their health, toward herself, by contrast, as already said, she was demanding and severe, always subjecting her frail body to every exertion, granting it neither food nor rest.

Immense was her desire for penance, which led her to mortify her own body with the most severe disciplines, through hairshirts and small chains.

Her heroic temperance also showed itself in her perfect mastery of herself and her passions: she never showed anger, even in the most difficult and unforeseen moments, always maintaining a state of calm and serenity.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, attests:

"... here I say that her life was admirable for its penance, and also for the skill with which she concealed it. Frequenting the house, I heard that she never ate meat or appetizing food; and I have reason to believe that she lived on nothing but herbs"227.

"... the expression then — 'I have always been a little beast' — I myself heard from her own lips. On the occasion of my remarks about food, she once answered me: 'But Father, these things are not necessary,' referring even to ordinary foods"228.

"She used to say: when the Sisters want to do penance, they can procure their own mortifications; the community must do things in an orderly way"229.

"... I had occasion to learn of the ardent desire the Servant of God had to use instruments of penance.

I remember having sometimes seen her bent over and drawn, like a suffering person, although she strove to show her usual cheerfulness"230.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, observes:

"... going sometimes to the Briuccia house, where she was Superior, and finding her at table with the other Sisters, I would see vegetable leaves on her plate — but of the kind that are thrown away. I recall that once she came to St. Xavier's Hospital, where I was Superior. We were at recreation and sweets were being handed out: she took a little out of obedience, but perhaps went to spit it out, since she immediately moved away from us"231.

"... the Servant of God had no bed of her own: she took her rest seated on a chair; but for the most part she spent the night before the Blessed Sacrament"232.

"... I confirm her indulgence and kindness in dealing with the Sisters, as well as her austerity toward herself"233.

"I know what is said here about the use of instruments of penance, which she kept hidden; but that one was once found on the occasion of her illness, at which she blushed.

... as to the extraordinary use of instruments of penance every Friday, I have heard it said, and I can attest that sometimes I too noticed, in her movements on Fridays, signs suggesting bodily suffering"234.

"I never saw her troubled or restless, even on extraordinary occasions that would have been enough to make her fly into a great rage"235.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, declares:

"Temperance, then, shaped her life: being most mortified, feeding on barely the simple necessities, when even that she managed to get"236.

Sister Anna Maria Teresa Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, testifies:

"... the Servant of God was most mortified.

That the Servant of God had no bed I heard from the Sisters: and, when she fell fatally ill, the Sisters said that for eleven years she had had no bed"237.

"I heard from the Sisters that she used instruments of penance, and that these were later found after her death.

I confirm having seen the Servant of God always calm and serene"238.

Fr. Giuseppe Palazzotto, the fifth witness, confirms what he saw and knows:

"... the Servant of God ate nothing but vegetables and herbs.

... I heard it said that she used hairshirts.

... I always saw her calm"239.

Sister Anna Elisa Scrò, the second witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, describes:

"... her heroic spirit of penance and mortification, to the point of feeding only on the community's table scraps and, at times, on the chicken feed"240.

Sister Anna Teresina Lo Bue, the third witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, summarizes:

"... characteristic marks of her spirituality were charity toward the poor and her spirit of penance and prayer, to the point that she preferred to sleep on the altar's step"241.

From the testimonies reported and the trial documents concerning Sister Anna del Salvatore's whole life, particularly her religious life, it stands out that the Servant of God always practiced the virtue of temperance in an excellent and heroic way, including in her mastery of herself, her passions, and her character. All the testimonies and documents present Sister Anna del Salvatore to us as a religious always serene, balanced, and happy, even in the most difficult moments and in the unforeseen situations in which she managed to maintain the greatest calm, even when she had to face complex or painful circumstances.

From some letters of Sister Anna del Salvatore to the Foundress Mother, Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno, we can clearly perceive the spirit of penance and mortification that animated the Servant of God.

"... My dearest Mother, may the good God reward you and grant you all the choicest graces your most generous and good heart could desire... Your great goodness and immense charity toward me, your most unworthy daughter, is too great...

I hear you tell me to rest at least four hours; yes, my Mother, I am most ready, and I already did so at once... My Mother, what sorrow... yes, what strong sorrow I feel; I see in this a strong punishment for my sins, and perhaps, indeed without perhaps, for the little profit I drew from it..."242.

"... My God! I cannot explain to you the sorrow I suffered in leaving you without being able to bid you farewell... for pity's sake, may this never happen again; this was the greatest punishment for me, and I recognize that I deserved it through so many unfaithfulnesses of mine, yes, and I deserve worse and far worse..."243.

In her report, Sister Anna Consolata Massimelli reveals to us:

"She was most mortified; and I, seeing her so wasted in her person, cunningly obliged her to eat the food the community provided, and she too cunningly kept trying to mortify her appetite...

At night she slept very little; in the raw cold of Ovada, she kept the window open while praying"244.

Sister Anna Nazaria Provera, too, extols the heroic temperance of the Servant of God and, in her report, among other things, says:

"She was temperate in character, always gentle, patient, mortified in touch; she almost never used a bed, contenting herself with a little sleep, taken uncomfortably on the step of the Altar, before the Blessed Sacrament. She mortified her appetite, always eating simple, scant kitchen fare and the like. Not even in times of illness did she allow herself delicate food, except when compelled by holy Obedience"245.

Sister Anna Del Consiglio Chiaramonte notes:

"The Servant of God was never seen upset, for she was of a gentle and meek character. She was most temperate and mortified in her food, always choosing for herself the coarsest and in small quantity. She allowed her body very little sleep, spending whole nights praying on her knees, or seeing to some task to relieve the Sisters, or else going to care for the sick at home.

For her own use she always chose garments worn out and discarded by the Sisters. She tamed her flesh with harsh penances, disciplines, hairshirts, and mortifications of every kind.

She was most modest in her eyes, always keeping them lowered, especially when she found herself conversing with persons of the opposite sex. She also always sought to mortify her hearing, and in general all her senses, never allowing her exhausted body the slightest relief"246.

From the report of Sister Anna Maristella Calderone we come to know that:

"In temperance, the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore attained heroism. Content with coarse and poor food, she felt joy when she could feed on nothing but a little hard, moldy bread; and, so that this act of hers would not be attributed to virtue, she used to say that bread was good for her stomach. The continual and wearisome travels and the inward mortifications of spirit completed the beautiful picture of her temperance"247.

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari, speaking of the Servant of God's temperance, writes:

"Gentle in word and manner, she was the living example of meekness, nor do I recall, in the short time I knew her, that she ever raised her voice over any small or great adversity that befell her. In her inspired mortification, in the necessary bodily restoratives — eating, drinking, sleeping — she was exceedingly temperate...

To the abstinences of food... corresponded that of sleep: ... she had no bed, her place of rest being the holy Tabernacle, and this alone is enough to show how watchful that exhausted body kept over the senses, subjecting them to the strength of spirit that made our athlete of the faith great. Her modest dress never distinguished her from the lowliest Sister in the house; simple and clean, without affectation, she loved nothing but to enrich the heart beneath the poverty of the woolens that clothed her. Sparing in speech, she was edifying in her brief words, in which divine teaching was always summed up; never did pride or vanity touch her speech..."248.

And Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi recalls:

"Most gentle in character and patient with everyone, she sometimes grew irritated when she saw God offended; she ate only once a day, for the whole time we were together, and, when she could, chose the worst for herself; ... in her face she always showed herself cheerful and content with everyone"249.

From Sister Anna Paolina Viani, too, we learn that the Servant of God:

"She was most mortified in everything; she never complained of anything, however much it caused her distress or pain; she bore everything with great calm, I would even say indifference, for she let nothing show; she was always in a pleasant and cheerful mood... one remained full of admiration for her mortification and for her humility in hiding her penances"250.

In conclusion, we can say that Sister Anna del Salvatore, in her exercise of the virtue of temperance, perfectly practiced the invitation of Sacred Scripture: "Do not follow your passions; restrain your desires" (Sir 18:30), aware that the true follower of Jesus Christ — fully drawn to him and given over to him — must "live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world" (Titus 2:12), aspiring above all to heavenly goods.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church, in no. 915, thus sums up the doctrine on the evangelical counsels as a path to the perfection of charity:

"The evangelical counsels, in their variety, are proposed to every disciple of Christ. The perfection of charity, to which all the faithful are called, entails for those who freely accept the vocation to consecrated life the obligation of practicing chastity in celibacy for the sake of the kingdom, poverty, and obedience. It is the profession of these counsels, within a permanent state of life recognized by the Church, that characterizes the life 'consecrated' to God."

Letting herself be guided by the Spirit in an unceasing journey of purification, the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore welcomed Christ's invitation to "share his experience as virgin, poor, and obedient, and showed the explicit desire of total conformity to him" (cf. Post-Synodal Apostolic Exhortation, Vita Consecrata, 18c).

Having entered religious life, she distinguished herself in the exercise of the virtues that characterize the Christi vivendi forma and daily lived out the demands proper to consecration: poverty, as the discovery of the Poor Christ, the sole treasure of her life; chastity, as unconditional adherence to the Bridegroom-Lamb and the capacity to love tenderly after the measure of Christ's heart; obedience, as the radical expression of Jesus's love for the Father's plan. Thus she made her own the attitudes of Jesus the Servant (the meek Lamb, silent before his shearer), the pivot of the Daughters of St. Anne's spirituality; and of Jesus who serves (humility, respect, gentleness, compassion).

But did she practice and fulfill heroically these sacred obligations, freely accepted on the day of her religious profession, so that the Church might now propose her as a model for those who, answering the divine call, wish to follow the path leading to perfection in charity? This precise question will be answered in the paragraphs that follow, in all justice and truth.

a) Heroic Poverty

The concept the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore had of poverty, as virtue and as vow, was truly demanding and gives us the measure of the spirit with which, from the very beginning of her religious life, she embraced this sacred duty of following the poor Jesus out of love for her brothers and sisters.

The Servant of God loved poverty and practiced it from childhood. We know her family was poor, and it was precisely from her parents and in the school of her family that Sister Anna del Salvatore learned to love poverty without ever showing any discomfort, but, always serene and cheerful, she helped out and was "modest in dress and bearing."

In the Report of the Historical Experts we read:

""With praiseworthy patience she bore the lack of things she often needed," relates the parish priest of Albareto, Don Tommaso Grilli, about her. And Orsolina Bottego attests that "to make a sacrifice of her life she ate almost always vegetables." Having entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, the Servant of God led a life of great penance. She took only one meal a day and also suffered some humiliation for being faithful to this choice"251.

Sister Anna del Salvatore's heroic poverty was evidenced above all in religious life, becoming her daily habitus, which showed through in every moment of her day.

"Sister Anna del Salvatore, walking in the footsteps of the divine Master, loved poverty as though in it she had found her rich treasure"252.

Desiring to imitate the Master who, poor among the poor, went about doing good to all, the Servant of God sincerely loved poverty and lived it in joyful simplicity of spirit, bearing clear and concrete witness that "God is man's only true wealth," and nourishing in herself — in real detachment, in solidarity, in availability, in unconditional service and in the sharing of goods — the same mind as Christ Jesus.

We read, in the Report of the Historical Experts:

"... The poor! They were indeed the person of Christ for our heroine; on them she lavished all her care with the fervor of one who wishes to please the beloved...

... she had grasped the value of asceticism in Christian life as a means of purification, of sharing in the condition of the poor, of identification with the Crucified Christ, and she never neglected it"253.

"... This virtue sets the person in her truth before God, in the condition of receiving everything from him as a gift, and it is an expression of interior poverty. Sister Anna del Salvatore truly followed the teaching of Jesus, 'Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart,' and always sought concealment"254.
