The Servant of God's correspondence, and especially the letters written to the Foundress Mother, is a continual account of the Community's material needs, which she faced always with great serenity and trust in Divine Providence.

She writes from Florence, on 16 March 1877:

"Dear beloved Mother,

... Jesus sees that I am an unruly little donkey, and so he thinks of everything himself. Yesterday the bread bill came to me, and I burst out laughing because I had only 30 (francs) and the bill was nearly 90 francs, but the Lord, so good, provided me with that and even more... So I am happy, because I think of nothing"255.

The Servant of God never allowed herself the slightest waste, and this spirit of poverty of hers was strongly passed on to all her Sisters.

Everything around the Servant of God breathed poverty, not only as to food but also in clothing. Her room was so poor that it lacked even the most necessary things, such as a nightstand and even a bed, which she considered a luxury.

"For her there was neither room nor bed. The Sister in charge of the linen, when changing her laundry, left it in the sacristy. Her food was a simple soup of vegetables, greens, or potatoes, in a single meal, at midday"256.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, declares:

"... she was most poor in spirit, always choosing the meanest things for herself, preferring to give the best to the Sisters: to such a degree that the Sisters themselves had to force her to use something of better quality. I recall that she would appeal to me so that the Sisters would not force her, using as a pretext that the most ill-fitting thing suited her better. I also recall that, to meet the needs of the young Community, I would offer some money: but she, on one occasion when she had no need of it, answered, refusing, with these words: Father, having no need of it, to accept it would seem to me greed"257.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, offering further details, attests:

"Of the Servant of God's love for poverty everyone knows: that she wore the shabbiest clothes is most certain; to such a degree that at her death truly wretched clothes of hers were found258.

... that she never wasted the Community's goods and belongings in the slightest, and with holy ingenuity sought to economize even in things that would otherwise have had no further use...

Of the poverty of her room, which lacked even the necessary things, even a bed, which for her, she said, would have been a luxury"259.

"... she liked to know that she ate by alms, and so she asked for alms, and this spirit of poverty she instilled in the Sisters, to whom she said, on going to dinner, that they should consider themselves poor, receiving their food by alms"260.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, confirms:

"Poverty she truly professed: dressing plainly, seeking no distinctions of any kind"261.

Sister Anna Elisa Scrò, the second witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, observes:

"The sense of truly heroic poverty... stands out from the fact that the Servant of God, within the religious Community, had no bed of her own and preferred to rest lying on the altar's step"262.

Sister Anna Gaetanina Zupone, the seventh witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, adds:

"... the characteristic marks of the Servant of God's spirituality are poverty of heart and motherly self-giving"263.

Mrs. Letizia Berni, the tenth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, specifies:

"... much was emphasized, about the Servant of God, concerning her life of poverty and sacrifice, of prayer and work"264.

Sister Anna Giuseppa Rovello, the twenty-second witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, affirms:

"Sister Anna del Salvatore, even as Provincial Superior, was most poor and mortified!"265.

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari, too, in her report, emphasizes:

"Her modest dress never distinguished her from the lowliest Sister in the house; simple and clean, without affectation, she loved nothing but to enrich her heart beneath the poverty of the woolens that covered her.

... Of her it could truly be said that she had no place to seek rest in the hours that follow the weariness of long labors"266.

The author of the first biography, who surely also knew Sister Anna del Salvatore personally, acquaints us with the profound spirit of poverty that the Servant of God fully expressed in her religious state:

"As for poverty, it is told that Sister Anna del Salvatore gave no thought to her clothing; anything suited her. The more patched a habit was, the dearer it was to her, and the Mother once had to oblige her to put on a new habit, because the one she had worn for years and years had patches and mendings one upon another. She would have gone about with her toes sticking out of her shoes, had not the sisters taken care to replace the unusable ones with a new pair; and it often happened that she did not notice the change, and on noticing it, took them off to give to another Sister... She called herself owner of nothing, considered herself a mere custodian of the Community's goods, and was most zealous about it.

Once she arrived at a house and, laughing, told how she had traveled with her companion in the livestock car, because she did not have enough money to lodge more comfortably"267.

Sister Anna del Salvatore, radically demanding of herself and aware of the obligation of poverty which she had freely and lovingly accepted with her vow, remained faithful to the spirit and practice of this virtue, living it to a truly eminent degree, not only as renunciation of earthly goods but also, and above all, as a means of identifying herself with God made flesh, the God who shows his true face in weakness, in pain, and in the crucifixion of the body; a means, therefore, of possessing the supreme Good.

b) Heroic Chastity

The conciliar norm contained in the decree Perfectae Caritatis recommends this counsel in a particularly forceful way and calls it a "distinguished gift of grace":

"Chastity, embraced for the sake of the kingdom of heaven as professed by religious, should be esteemed as a distinguished gift of grace. For it frees the human heart in a unique way so as to enkindle it with greater charity toward God and toward everyone, and it stands as a particular sign of heavenly goods and the most suitable means by which religious generously dedicate themselves to the service of God and to works of the apostolate" (no. 12).

The Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore, even then, reflected in herself what the Second Vatican Council would later define. She loved and practiced chastity, considering it a great gift of God that freed her heart from all that was of the world, so as to consecrate herself without hindrance to the pure love of God and of all her needy brothers and sisters.

In the virtue of chastity she grew with spontaneity, for all the means for its exercise and growth were cultivated by her: prayer, mortification, the Eucharist, and modesty.

Sister Anna del Salvatore sought in every way to preserve this beautiful virtue, keeping even the slightest impurity far from herself.

In the report of Sister Anna Maristella Calderone we read:

"Just as she was poor, so too she was chaste, watching over herself to flee from anything that might arouse in her soul a thought less than pure"268.

Don Tommaso Grilli, parish priest of Albareto, writing in 1890 an account of the Servant of God, also relates a confidence made by the Servant of God to one of his parishioners:

"Before entering religious life, she returned to Albareto to greet her relatives and companions and had a familiar conversation with Mrs. Bosi Valentina, her confidante, who assures me with certainty (and is a person worthy of belief) that Orsi also spoke to her of the dances which, in private homes in Albareto, she had sometimes happened to attend, at the invitation and urging of some companions, and told her that, every time, after such amusements, she always found herself regretful and so repentant that she was driven to weep"269.

From the two biographies, by Onorata Colli and by Frati Roberta Cecilia, it emerges how the Servant of God practiced the virtue of chastity in an extraordinary way from her most tender age:

"Our Marianna was much loved throughout the village for the rare gifts with which she was endowed. She had a most gentle temperament and a calm spirit; she was without vanity in dress and bearing; she knew nothing of pretense, and, though she enjoyed being in cheerful company with girls her own age, she was most reserved in her conduct, and in conversation never let slip an improper word"270.

"Everyone notices her goodness and her joy in living, the serenity with which she faces sacrifices and hardships, the living faith that animates her daily life. Her friends seek out her company: they gladly stay with her, for she has a great heart, is so gentle and modest, and always cheerful"271.

The Servant of God was always most reserved; never did an act or a word less than correct escape her, and nothing was ever noticed that betrayed, even in the slightest, the innocence of her virginal heart.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, so testifies:

"Of the Servant of God's love for chastity, I can speak of her reserve in dealing with people.

Never did I hear from the Servant of God's mouth a word that in the least alluded to anything that might harm the splendor of this beautiful virtue.

I know all that is said here of her frequenting the sacraments and all else (sic; that is, whatever else) served to guard her holy purity.

These exhortations to the beautiful virtue given to the Sisters were something truly edifying for the whole community"272.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, attests:

"Chastity shone in her through the modesty of her conduct and in her most reserved manner of dealing with people"273.

His Excellency Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, testifies:

"She was most modest in all her actions, and no one could ever have the slightest suspicion of wrongdoing about her conduct, even when she found herself amid the exercise of public charity"274.

The Servant of God not only zealously guarded chastity as a "distinguished gift of grace," but lived it as an experience of joy and freedom, giving continual witness of serenity, balance, love, maturity, and universality.

"Her heart was a burning furnace," writes Sister Anna Gregoria Poppelman in her report, "and it was enough to speak with her of things of perfection to feel one's heart catch fire with holy affections"275.

"Although the Servant of God was so modest and reserved in her conduct," states Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte, "people, edified by such rare modesty, held her in such high esteem"276.

"Sister Anna del Salvatore," we read in the Report of the Historical Experts, "was a shining example of faithful following of the Lord and of generous, boundless charity toward her brothers and sisters, because in her life she entrusted herself entirely to the Lord and let herself be guided and shaped by him, growing continually in the knowledge and love of Jesus, and continually widening her capacity for concrete, effective self-giving"277.

And "La Sicilia cattolica," in the obituary published on 12 June 1885:

"She was such that, merely drawing near her, one was taken as if by enchantment, not knowing what to admire first in her — her deep humility or her dignified bearing; the gentleness of her manners or the sobriety of her speech; the strength of a lion or the meekness of a lamb; the zeal that consumes or the charity that has compassion: She was one of those beings who shine with a light clear, beautiful, consoling, yet at the same time mysterious and indefinable, like the very light of God..."278.

Though in language typical of the late nineteenth century, Fr. Gaetano Gabriele, who delivered the funeral oration at the solemn obsequies of the Servant of God, thus extolled the virtue of chastity exercised in a heroic way by Sister Anna del Salvatore:

"What shall we say of the beautiful virtue of virginal innocence that adorned the great soul of the illustrious departed? She knows full well that such a virtue makes men like the angels, and that virgins, marked by a mysterious seal upon the brow, form the Immaculate Lamb's guard of honor, and follow him wherever he goes, and sing a mysterious song that only they are permitted to sing. And she, zealous to keep unsullied this priceless pearl of heaven, not unaware of the burden of Adam borne by whoever is born of woman, though she had always lived most innocent, nonetheless chose to build herself a hedge, to render herself invulnerable to the attacks of the world, the flesh, and the devil: a hedge woven of the voluntary mortifications that, for love of her God, she chose to add to the austerities of the rule and the precepts of the Institute"279.

c) Heroic Obedience

According to the witnesses' depositions and the trial documents, it emerges that, on the path of obedience, the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore sought "to attain the measure of the full stature of Christ," as the decree Perfectae Caritatis proposes (no. 14), carrying out the will of God in order to become holy.

Among all the qualities and virtues that adorned the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore, obedience shone forth in a particular way, a virtue always lived with joy and fidelity, without the slightest reluctance toward any disposition of her Superiors.

Even in her final illness this extraordinary spirit of obedience stood out in her, as she carried out everything she was commanded.

Sister Anna del Salvatore was extremely observant of all the Rules of the Institute and wanted her Sisters, too, to follow her in this commitment.

When she became Superior and then Provincial of numerous Houses in Sicily, she gave an admirable example of obedience. A most faithful daughter to the Foundress Mother, a single sign expressing her wish was enough for it to be carried out at once with promptness and the full adherence of her heart.

In the Circular Letter of the co-founder Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore and the foundress Rosa Gattorno, written to the whole Institute the year after the Servant of God's death, we read:

"In her there was a heroic obedience. In the Mother she perceived and loved Jesus Christ, so that a single sign from her was enough for her to be found wherever the Mother called her"280.

For her, obedience was everything, declares Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness:

"That the Servant of God had a great spirit of obedience was evident from the fact that, when the Mother General gave orders, she had them carried out punctually, saying: the Mother wants it so, and so it must be done... I too can attest that she not only instilled obedience, but demanded it"281.

Even in circumstances difficult for her, obedience was always prompt. This is the case, recounted by several witnesses, of her prompt obedience to an order of the Mother General, despite being very ill, to go to Trapani to settle a matter.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, testifies:

"... out of obedience, she accompanied the Sister to Trapani while burning with fever. On returning, she took to her bed. Then, out of obedience to the Mother General, who had written to her about it, she, in this grave state of health, as I was told, rose from bed and went to the chapel to pray, the Mother General hoping for her recovery; instead, a few days later she died"282.

"... a benefactor, namely Msgr. Briuccia, in whose palazzo the Community was lodged, having sent her, in her grave state of health, a quarter of a chicken, she turned to me, saying: 'Father, I absolutely cannot take this food.' I understood she said this because she did not eat meat, having always abstained from it. I answered: 'Let it be.' But she added: 'But Msgr. Briuccia will ask me about it, and if I do not taste it, he might take offense.' So I replied: 'You may take a tiny bit, to please him.' She made a gesture of resignation with her hands and eyes. Returning afterward, I asked her whether she had taken the chicken, and she answered: 'I took it; it went in, but it will not come out again.' She having died shortly after, I understood the meaning of her words"283.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, testifies:

"The Servant of God was most obedient, even to the point of sacrifice. And this I know from many occasions.

This spirit of conformity to the wishes of the Mother General, too, was known to everyone, and I attest to it"284.

"Her obedience toward the Mother General, even in matters distasteful to her, we know and we attest.

This fact of her obedience, imposed by the Mother General without the latter knowing the grave state of the Servant of God's illness, is such as to cause amazement. She left with a fever of forty degrees. She went, settled the matter; but, back in Palermo, she took to her bed, from which she never rose again.

It is true that, in her final illness, she obeyed the instructions of the doctor and of the Sisters, both as to the medicines and as to the manner of carrying out the prescriptions"285.

Fr. Enrico Filiti, the third witness, reveals:

"As to obedience toward her Superiors, I take it for granted, because she did nothing that was not in keeping with the holy Rule and the orders of her Superiors"286.

Rev. Duilio Odoidio Schiavetta, the twentieth witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, confirms:

"... her readiness toward her Sisters and her total obedience toward her Superiors even in a precarious state of health. And, further, her spirit of sacrifice exercised in a heroic way"287.

The Servant of God obeyed gladly, without reluctance, with a smile on her lips, making no remark, thinking that she was obeying God himself.

"Truly, all of us who were close to her," adds Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi further, "would have wished to imitate her in this noble virtue of obedience, so much did she make it appear pleasant and easy"288.

The first biographer of the Servant of God, Onorata Colli, wrote:

"Accustomed to obeying her parents, she had no difficulty obeying the Teacher. She knew that God had chosen her to represent him and to be the instrument through which his holy Will was made known to her, and she held every word of hers sacred and would not have drawn back even before the gravest obstacle when she had to carry out an order of hers, which for her was inviolable law; therefore she obeyed, obeyed always without reluctance and without complaint, rather glad to be able to give her Superiors proof of her perfect submission"289.

We better understand Sister Anna del Salvatore's virtue of obedience by looking closely at her correspondence with the Foundress Mother, Blessed Rosa Gattorno, to whose directives the Servant of God submitted in every activity, every need, every slightest uncertainty. Her most recurrent words were, in fact: "I would like to ask you whether you could give me permission to..."

The Servant of God, even as a superior, never took any initiative without first having consulted the Mother General and asked her permission:

"Now I beg you to tell me how I should behave, that is, how I should answer Father Cusmano..."; "I beg you, out of charity, if you can, to tell me whether I should continue like this or not, and likewise, as regards the Baroness, whether I should keep on sending the sisters to take her out, or not..."290.

And whenever she did take some initiative without the necessary permission, she would write at once to ask forgiveness, as in the case of the telegram sent to her dying brother, who wished to speak with her:

"Mother, I beg you out of charity to forgive such boldness of mine, for at that moment I did not know what I was doing"291.

Reading these letters, at first glance one might believe the Servant of God was always indecisive, weak of character, and so on, whereas on closer study one realizes it was her submission to the will of God, expressed through the will of the Foundress Mother, being deeply aware of her spiritual daughterhood; and she obeyed the Mother so that harmony and uniformity of purpose and action might reign in the Institute.

"Dearest Mother, I come with this my first letter to tell you that I found myself quite confused, dear Mother, because, saying to myself: poor thing, so incapable, how shall I manage, though I gladly do the obedience. Dear Mother, I tell the Lord to do it for me, that all will go well; then I tell the Holy Mother, who guides me, that for love of God she may make me do everything well...

Mother, as to the fast, I tell you that now I am being lazy about it... that it is better to work as I did before, to go begging; but do with me as you think best: ready, obedient to your signs"292.

"Dear beloved Mother, as great as was the joy I felt on receiving your so longed-for letter, just as painful was it to read it. Oh God, what sorrow, what great pain it was for me to hear that in this community there is so much disorder because of me. My God, what heartbreak... Ah, my dear Mother, if this happens through my fault, you, so good, may remove me so as not to give this scandal, and then this holy community will flourish and spread its most beautiful branches throughout this beautiful city; however, I am ready to do in everything and for everything whatever you command me, and, if I had to remain my whole life long in this community, I would gladly do so, provided my dear Mother is content..."293.

Also, and especially, in moments of difficulty or trial, the Servant of God always remained faithful and ready to obey any decision and order of the Mother General.

"Ah! What sorrow has just now come upon me, quite unexpectedly. And how could it be that I should not wish to do the obedience, when I am so glad to be able to see you? And how could I go on living if, even for a single moment, such a thought had come to my mind? My God! After so much joy felt on receiving the news of coming to make the holy Exercises, must I feel this strong sorrow of having my dear Mother oblige me by obedience...

... I am always, and will always be, yours, and I am content to do your will and not mine; if I must come sooner, I shall be the more content"294.

Convinced that obedience carried out in communion with the will of God has also the value of expiation, Sister Anna del Salvatore, while obeying the Mother's precepts, sets forth with humble confidence her thought, which leads her to consider herself unworthy of such attentions and care — a cause of real mortification for her.

"I hear you tell me to rest at least four hours. Yes, my Mother, I am most ready, and I already did so at once... Ah! My Mother, what sorrow... yes, what strong sorrow I feel; I see in this a strong punishment for my sins, and perhaps, indeed without perhaps, for the little profit I drew from it..."295.

The first Theological Censor writes:

"Outwardly, the Servant of God's extreme humility takes shape in the uninterrupted exercise of an absolute and undivided obedience to the rule and to the Institute's Superiors, especially the Foundress, toward whom she nurtures and cultivates a special veneration...

Obedience is lived as the royal road to the realization and enjoyment of communion"296.

The second Theological Censor notes:

"This full rootedness in God through prayer not only gives her strength in fulfilling her duties but confers on her the drive of an unshakeable obedience, founded on humility...

Well rooted in her are the convictions that the will of God is made known and followed by obeying the Foundress and the Rule, awaiting from her Superiors the necessary correction"297.

Besides her parents and the Foundress Mother, Sister Anna del Salvatore was supremely obedient to the representatives of God: the Pope, the Bishops, priests, spiritual directors, and in general any superior invested with authority. This can be seen in her conduct and behavior during her stay in Florence toward the Archbishop and the priests she came into contact with, and later with the Bishops, priests, and heads of the various Works and Institutions in Sicily.

Exemplary in the heroic practice of this virtue, we may well say that the Servant of God also became, for all her Sisters, a true "teacher of obedience."

d) Heroic Humility

St. Peter the Apostle addresses to all believing followers of Jesus the Savior, whether they belong to the hierarchy or to the faithful people, this call and invitation:

"Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble" (1 Pt 5:5).

From what we have already seen and come to know of our Servant of God's life and activities, we may easily conclude that Sister Anna del Salvatore knew how to clothe herself in the garment of a servant and the garment of humble service. She was truly humble in her way of being and acting, always behaving as though she were the last among all the Daughters of St. Anne. For this the Lord poured out his grace upon her and blessed her abundantly.

In the Report of the Experts "in re historica" we read:

"The Servant of God's so luminous faith was accompanied by a vivid sense of humility.

This virtue sets the person in her truth as a creature before God, in the condition of receiving everything from him as a gift, and is an expression of interior poverty. Sister Anna del Salvatore truly followed the teaching of Jesus, 'Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart,' and always sought concealment.

... Her letters are all imbued with sentiments of humility.

... When she judges that she has erred, she humbly asks forgiveness and asks to be assigned a penance.

... deep humility led the Servant of God to bear with serenity being unjustly accused and to forgo defending herself, seeking her defense in God alone. Although her conscience reproaches her with nothing, she asks forgiveness for the displeasure she has involuntarily caused..."298.

Also of interest is the opinion of the first Theological Censor, the Very Rev. Don Rosario La Delfa, who, having read and examined the Servant of God's letters, expresses himself thus on Sister Anna del Salvatore's virtue of humility:

"The virtue that most illuminates the exercise of the Servant of God's spiritual gifts, and on which all her other interior and exterior dispositions wrought in her by grace are firmly based, is certainly humility. There is no portion of her writings from which the consistency and solidity of this fundamental condition does not shine through. It is visible especially from a twofold perspective, the inward and the outward.

Inwardly, this virtue acts as a disposition toward perfection in the awareness of the limits of one's own nature, that is, in a situation of constant dependence on the grace of God, which alone can supply what is lacking to one's own inadequacy. It generates an unconditional readiness to cooperate with God so that his will for good and his power of salvation may be shown forth in others [...].

Outwardly," the Theological Censor continues, reaffirming what he already said of obedience, "the Servant of God's extreme humility takes shape in the uninterrupted exercise of an absolute and undivided obedience to the rule and to the Institute's superiors, especially the Foundress, toward whom she nurtures and cultivates a special veneration"299.

The whole life of Sister Anna del Salvatore — those who knew her affirm — was an expression of the heroic exercise of the virtue of humility; for this reason this virtue is greatly emphasized in all the testimonies gathered in the Processes and in the reports written by her Sisters.

His Most Excellent and Reverend Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, affirms:

"Of her humility I can say that this virtue was her hallmark: the very word Pride filled her with horror, unable to believe that one could be proud"300.

So Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, sees her:

"The Servant of God's humility was such that she was incapable, I do not say of writing or saying things that would redound to her praise, but even of thinking them"301.

"Her whole life is sown with sentiments of true humility on the part of the Servant of God. She often said that she was the last and quite unnecessary; that others would have known how to do better than she; that she was the last in the house; she called herself the Community's donkey.

Of the expressions of humility of the Servant of God it can be said that they were her whole life. It was her mirror...

... when she was given words of praise, she was mortified by them, and instead spoke words of contempt about herself.

... That she instilled sentiments of humility in everyone, I too could hear, to my great edification and that of others"302.

Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, attests:

"Nothing of pride or vanity did I observe in her during the time I knew her; on the contrary, the truest and most sincere humility was revealed in every one of her acts or words"303.

Sister Anna Serafina Gregory, the sixth witness, specifies:

"I saw in her a deep humility; she placed herself beneath everyone's feet. And this I saw and judged to be something true and never affected: sincere, as the saints speak and act. This was the esteem that I and others held for the Servant of God"304.

Sister Anna del Salvatore spoke humbly with all her Sisters and received every correction, piece of advice, and warning with gratitude. She considered herself the most ignorant and inept of all, judged herself with great severity, accusing herself of being full of faults, and implored whoever it might be to give her suggestions. Her advice, always given with extreme humility, never mortified anyone. The Servant of God's heroic humility also showed itself in her readiness to carry out, unceasingly and with a cheerful and serene spirit, the humblest and most repugnant tasks.

The witness Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino further declares:

"... the Servant of God was most humble.

That the Servant of God, at home, did the lowliest tasks, even that of doing the laundry, I heard from the Sisters.

That the Servant of God sought out humiliations could be seen in every one of her acts..."305.

And Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, relates:

"... from having heard it said, the slander raised against her was aired in Florence, on the occasion when, in Piacenza, the Superiors of the various Houses had gathered to make the spiritual exercises. It was said that the Servant of God had spoken in the Community words not respectful toward the Foundress Mother and her family; to such a degree that it was proposed to take away her veil and send her away. Informed of this, the Servant of God did not wish to defend herself, but, bowing her head in true humility, said: 'If God wills this humiliation of me, I am ready to undergo it'"306.

From the testimonies of the Supplementary Diocesan Inquiry as well, in which the witnesses testifying do so de auditu (by hearsay), it is evident that the moral virtue of humility was peculiar and predominant in Sister Anna del Salvatore's life.

So testifies Sister Anna Teresina Lo Bue, the third witness of the Supplementary Inquiry:

"Of the Servant of God's life I admired above all her humble resignation shown when she was threatened by our Foundress Mother with expulsion from the Institute as a result of slander. Therefore, the virtue that most stands out in her life is humility"307.

Sister Anna Giuseppa Rovello, the twenty-second witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, who did not know the Servant of God but had as her Superior a sister who had known Sister Anna del Salvatore directly, affirms in her deposition:

"The virtue of humility strikes me as significant in the Servant of God's life. In this regard I recall that our Superior used to tell us what Sister Anna del Salvatore had affirmed in the episode of the slander: Mother Rosa herself must be the one to take my veil from me! And I will stand by the Institute's gate to beg alms so as to keep helping the Institute"308.

Sister Anna Gaetanina Zupone, the seventh witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, declares:

"The Servant of God was marked by her great humility and spirit of sacrifice, both in the community where she lived and toward the very poor..."309.

Rev. Giuseppe Conti, the twenty-fifth witness (the first ex officio) of the Supplementary Inquiry, confirms:

"... what strikes me most is her dedication to the humblest tasks"310.

Sister Anna Silvina Margiotta attests:

"In the Servant of God I particularly admired her humility and her charity, virtues she exercised in Sicily too, when she was appointed Provincial Superior311.

... With great humility and charity she offered herself for the care of the sick at home"312.

Mr. Pietro Spanò, the twenty-first witness of the Supplementary Inquiry, emphasizes:

"What strikes me most about the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi is her humility and her unconditional dedication to others, particularly to the needy and the suffering, as well as her profound sense of endurance and submission before the adversities of her existence"313.

Her conduct regarding the slander is also described in the Report of the Historical Experts. There we read:

"Her deep humility led the Servant of God to bear with serenity being unjustly accused and to forgo defending herself, seeking her defense in God alone. Although her conscience reproaches her with nothing, she asks forgiveness for the displeasure she has involuntarily caused and, faced with the possible dismissal from the Institute, confides to Sister Anna Costanza Cenni: I will put up no resistance; I will do as Isaac did, who made the sacrifice of his life. I will lay my head on the Mother's knees, as Isaac laid himself on the bundle of wood; let her do as she wishes, I will put up no resistance, but if I must leave the Institute, I will try to do all the good I can for the Institute"314.

And this also follows from what the Servant of God herself expresses to the Foundress Mother, Blessed Rosa Gattorno, in her letter of 21 February 1878:

"Dear Mother, I assure you that even had you not obliged me by obedience, I would have told you the plain truth. Oh my Jesus, how glad I am that you let all the blame rain down on me and leave him free and unburdened... Oh God, for my great sins everything is too little. It only grieves me, oh my beloved Mother, that I am the ungrateful and cruel one who makes you languish. Oh Mother, if I may still call you Mother, it seems that hell has been unleashed against me"315.

The Servant of God rejoiced at being humbled and reproved unjustly, and was content with humiliations, thinking that Jesus had suffered something far more humiliating.

No different is the spirit of deep humility perceived in reading through the Servant of God's correspondence and the testimonies gathered in the reports written by her Sisters or sent by other people.

Let us read, in this regard, what the priest Don Petronio Russo, an eyewitness to an episode that occurred in Adernò (today Adrano), relates:

"... This poorhouse was administered by the confraternity of charity, of which Fr. Benedetto Ciancio was President... He imprudently requested... an office that the Provincial Mother could not and should not grant according to the Institute's rules. Fr. Ciancio pressed the matter until he heaped insults and abuse upon her. But she did not react at all; rather, she humbly accepted the abuse and remained steadfast in upholding the Institute's good name.

It seemed fitting to me, as parish priest, confessor of the Sisters, and one of the leading citizens of Adernò, to apologize to her for the insult she had suffered. She, however, quite calm and smiling, kept repeating: that Father said words I deserved. Besides, she added... I am the servant of the Daughters of St. Anne"316.

Sister Anna Nazaria Provera writes:

"The Servant of God showed no esteem for herself at all. She spoke very little, and only out of necessity accepted any special consideration. She hid from the eyes of men the good she did, content only to please the Lord"317.

Sister Anna Del Consiglio Chiaramonte notes:

"The Servant of God never showed any wish to be esteemed, still less praised, and, an enemy of self-regard, fled from praise as from the infernal serpent. She held a rather low opinion of herself and of worldly things, and if she accepted the office of Provincial Superior, it was only to obey her Superiors, who imposed it on her by holy Obedience"318.

In this regard, we also quote some expressions drawn from the Servant of God's correspondence with some of the Sisters.

On 28 July 1884, she writes from Palermo to Sister Anna della Mercede:

"... superior beloved by the heart of God, I would ask you a great favor...: not to call me Provincial anymore, ah!... for pity's sake, I beg you not to give me that so sad a name... for me. So, you who are so good, I am most certain and sure that you will wish to console me"319.

Still from Palermo, replying to Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega, then secretary general, on 17 February 1885 she writes:

"... I have really done nothing, nothing, only your great goodness, which accepts everything, but ah!... for charity's sake, I beg you not to use with me certain expressions... My God, my heart... is worse than a tigress and is a volcano full of every iniquity... And besides, that I should have virtue... Good God, what confusion such words are for me!...

Only by the great mercy of the good God and the very great goodness of our dear Mother has it brought me to this point, of being able to live in community, and the goodness of the Sisters, who with such charity put up with me; for the rest, I am nothing but an abyss of iniquity..."320.

Sister Anna Maristella Calderone, in her report, says further of her:

"All these virtues shone with an even more splendid beauty, because accompanied by that simple, unaffected humility, free of ostentation, that spiritual masters have always held to be the foundation of holiness"321.

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari, too, recalls:

"I never heard her speak of herself, except to show her own lowliness, for I often heard her repeat that she was good for nothing — and if some occasion ever revealed traits of her virtue, or if the Sisters spoke of some benefit obtained by someone through the Sister's intercession, and she heard it, she was there, ready, with the humility that seeks to efface itself, to cut the conversation short in the middle, but so gently, without affectation, with the indifference of one who regards as easy the success of an undertaking that seems difficult"322.

Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi confirms:

"She always held herself to be the meanest of creatures and took care that her virtues and merits remain hidden both from her Sisters and from everyone"323.

And Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno confirms this, who, in her personal writings, praises and deeply esteems the Servant of God for her intense spirit of humility:

"She had a profound humility; she always held herself the lowliest of creatures. Oh, how great she was in the sight of God! Oh sweet love!"324.

In summary, we report what Fr. Enrico Filiti, the Servant of God's confessor, chose to write to the Foundress Mother on 7 July 1885:

"Holy soul! You were deeply humble to the very end of your life... Reverend Mother, I would not know how to describe in words the virtues that the lamented Superior practiced in heroic degree; it was a hidden virtue, yet apparent to all who drew near her, even for the first time; in vain she strove to hide herself, to such a degree that, at certain moments and in certain cases, she wished to make herself look ridiculous; this ingenious device was of no avail — she was the violet that spread the fragrance of its scent while hidden beneath the leaves"325.

Such and so profound did the humility of our Sister Anna del Salvatore show itself to be!...

It is well known that charisms supra naturam gratis a Deo concessa326 testify, albeit indirectly, to the abundance of virtues with which privileged souls who are friends of God are filled.

In confirmation of her most sublime practice of virtue, Sister Anna del Salvatore was adorned by God with supernatural gifts. Imbued with a very great faith and a boundless love for God, she was often seen by her Sisters falling into ecstasy while at prayer; and she was also endowed with the gift of prophecy, foreseeing future events, both joyful and sorrowful. Many were the prophecies concerning the Foundress Mother.

From the testimonies of the two Processes of Palermo, the ordinary and the supplementary diocesan one, as well as from the extrajudicial acts, there emerges the presence of these exceptional charisms in the Servant of God's life.

His Excellency the Most Rev. Msgr. Ignazio Zuccaro, the first witness, reveals:

"... in her final illness, when her death was not feared, and when another religious, afflicted at the same time with typhoid fever, to whom I myself had administered the Holy Viaticum, was also ill, the Servant of God, who constantly asked about the sick sister, on hearing that it was not serious, immediately answered: 'You are hiding the truth: but I tell you she will live and I will die.' Indeed, the sister recovered shortly afterward and had been so gravely ill that she remembered neither her confession nor the Viaticum; while the Servant of God, a few days later, truly died"327.

Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, the second witness, for her part, relates:

"I have heard it said that the Servant of God would fall into ecstasy, that she was found absorbed in God in prayer to the point that it took effort to rouse her, and so many other things that savor of the supernatural"328.

"This matter of the increase of the two hundred lire she needed, I heard told by a Sister, who relates that, a young postulant having presented herself to her with an envelope containing eighty lire, the Servant of God told her that she needed more than double that, and that she should go and set the envelope before the Sacrament, behind the Gloria card, and pray. What happened was that, on taking back the envelope, it was found to contain two hundred lire more"329.

Sister Anna M. T. Patti di Sorrentino, the fourth witness, confirms:

"... the Servant of God herself told me that, when she received alms, she would place the envelopes before the Blessed Sacrament; the Sisters later told me that the money was always found multiplied"330.

Sister Anna Serafina Gregory, the sixth witness, testifies:

"Of the gift of prophecy I can speak from my own experience, for I often pressed her, wanting to know my future, and she told me that I would become a Daughter of St. Anne. I confess, however, that at that time I had no thought at all of embracing that Institute, also because I saw the austere life the Servant of God led...; I heard it told by one of the Sisters, namely Sister Anna Amante La Barbera, who, invited by the Servant of God while still a lay person, spent the night together with her in the religious House, saw her rise from the ground, caught up in the heavenly love that flooded her heart. And it was after this wondrous event that the good Sister La Barbera embraced the Institute, in which she perseveres to this day"331.

Let us read, however, the account of the episode in Sister Anna Amante La Barbera's own report:

"I went to her at the appointed hour, and when the sisters had already gone to rest, she led me into the Chapel, before the altar on which stood a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes, and we prayed, prayed a great deal, close to one another; she then prayed with a fervor I cannot describe; she seemed absorbed! When suddenly I see her slowly rising from the ground, and while I, astonished, watched her and almost tried to hold her back, I see that she has reached the statue and, in sweet ecstasy, remained close to the dear Blessed Virgin!... I, with an instinctive gesture, held myself back, fearing she might fall on me, and I watched her and called to her!... After a while, slowly, she came back down to the ground, and, as one awakening, she looks at me and says: 'You have seen! For you the Lord allowed this, to convince you that he wants you for himself; are you convinced of it? But woe, woe to you if you speak of what you have seen!...'"332.

Sister Anna Irene Carmeli, herself a witness to several episodes, also recounts:

"The Servant of God, visiting the hospital in that town [Castelvetrano], found there a poor sick woman struggling between life and death. The woman then commended herself to the good Sister, begging her to obtain her healing from God. Sister Anna del Salvatore remained silent a while, then, looking up to heaven, added: Daughter, ask the Lord rather for the salvation of your soul, for there is no hope whatsoever for the health of your body. For two days she did not cease to comfort the sick woman, until she persuaded her to receive the Most Holy Sacraments. That poor woman died in God's grace, calm and tranquil. It was learned afterward that for many years she had not approached the Altar"333.

Likewise, in the trial documents the supernatural gifts of Sister Anna del Salvatore are brought to light; and in some letters sent to the Foundress Mother Anna Rosa Gattorno, at least three prophecies made by Sister Anna del Salvatore concerning the Blessed herself stand out.

- Writing on 5 December to the Foundress Mother, she assures her that her little niece Noni will be well:

"Yes, Mother, the Most Holy Virgin loves you greatly, so she will watch over her, and Noni will be well"334;

and in a letter of 1884 she reassures her that her brother will not die:

"My God, what sorrow! But your sorrow, my Mother, grieves me even more. Yes, unfortunately it is all true, but I assure you, in the name of the Most Holy Virgin, that your Brother will not die, no; indeed I hope the Most Holy Virgin will not even let him fall ill, and, should he fall ill, he will recover quickly, yes, quickly..."335.

- Also in a letter fragment, probably from 1885, we find prophecies that concern the Foundress Mother directly and that have largely come true:

"Right now I would like to explain something to you, and it is that you, my Mother, will die — if I am not mistaken — will die in Rome, and your body will not decay, so that the worms will have nothing to do, and afterward you will not, no, be buried at San Lorenzo, but we will have the good fortune of having you with us... Great crowds will come to obtain graces and will obtain them... afterward you will be placed among the founders, in St. Peter's. Ah!... how well off you will be"336.

Indeed, Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno died in Rome, and although she was buried at the Verano, she was later transferred to the Generalate House, and her body remains incorrupt. She was beatified on 9 April 2000 by the Supreme Pontiff John Paul II.

Ivi si ricorda come il Moreau de Saint Méry [Mederic Louis Elie (1750-1819), diplomatico e storico francese, amministratore generale degli Stati Parmensi per conto di Napoleone Bonaparte negli anni 1802-1805] osservasse, in un rapporto del 1805, «che la proporzione dei membri del clero che esercitava "funzioni religiose" era inferiore di coloro che si limitavano a vivere "del prodotto delle loro messe" o lavoravano come istitutori e amministratori». Si riportano anche alcuni dati di notevole interesse: così, si riferisce che «nel 1812 su 1.566 preti presenti in diocesi [di Piacenza], ben 324 erano giudicati incapaci di essere impiegati utilmente nel ministero» (p. 271) e si indica il numero delle ordinazioni, sempre nella diocesi di Piacenza: «Se nel '700 la media delle ordinazioni sacerdotali superava spesso i 40 sacerdoti all'anno [...], nel primo decennio del [XIX] secolo [...] avevano raggiunto la cifra di 261.
